## README.md philosophy (top-level)

The README frames Claude Code as **one infrastructure layer among many**, in the same table row-for-row as shell config, git config, Angular CLI config, Node/pnpm/Nx toolchain, and VS Code — "Claude Code (CLI, plugins, skills, settings) | `claude/` | `install/claude-setup.sh`." Concretely, the stated design rules are: (1) settings are seeded once, never clobbered afterward, because Claude Code owns that file at runtime; (2) the permission seed is deliberately static/untemplated and identical on both machine profiles, explicitly preserving a prompt-gate on code-egress commands "on personal and work alike"; (3) on `machine = work`, the Claude Code **binary** is intentionally left out of auto-install — Accenture's Enterprise (no-training) install is used instead, and the repo only layers plugins/skills/settings on top of it, under an explicit caveat to "confirm what's sanctioned before using it on client code"; (4) skills are versioned bidirectionally (`sync-skills-to-repo.sh` snapshots live edits back into the repo, mirroring chezmoi's own edit/apply/re-add cycle). In short: Claude Code is managed as reproducible, idempotent, self-updating personal infrastructure — not as an app with one-off settings.

## Personal vs. work split

`.chezmoi.toml.tmpl` prompts once for a single `machine` value (`personal`/`work`, default `personal`) plus a per-machine git `email`, while `name` stays constant; `dot_gitconfig.tmpl` then templates `[user] name/email` straight from those two chezmoi values — so one repo produces one Marcel identity but a different git author email (and, per the README, different tool-install behavior — Vercel CLI/Postman/Docker and Claude-Code-auto-install are personal-only) depending on which profile answered the prompt.

## The distinction that matters for the playbook

The `manndotfiles/claude/` layer is Marcel's personal, global **operating configuration for the tool itself** — owned and authored by one person, living in `~/.claude/` outside any repo, identical across every client and every codebase he opens Claude Code in. It governs *how the tool behaves for him* (what it's allowed to run unprompted, which plugins/skills are loaded, the default effort dial, the statusline). A project's shared-rules layer (e.g., zimmermann-pwa's `.claude/` + `AGENTS.md`) is the opposite in kind: it's authored and version-controlled collectively by a team, lives inside one specific repo, is scoped only to that codebase, and encodes *domain and process knowledge* (file-protection tiers, component scaffolding conventions, Contentful sync rules, PR/release checklists) that any contributor — human or AI — working in that repo must follow, regardless of who they are. One is "how I run this tool, everywhere, forever"; the other is "what this codebase requires of anyone working in it, right now." Note for accuracy: neither layer, as inspected, contains the specific tone/anti-agreeableness prose the playbook describes — that instruction, if it exists at all, isn't committed in this repo.

## Research complete. Findings below, organized by your 10 questions, then consolidated corrections and undocumented capabilities.

---

### 1. Two-squad structure — `.claude/rules/squadA.md` + `.claude/rules/squadB.md`

**Real equivalent exists, but it directly contradicts four other sources in the repo — this is the single most important correction for the rewrite.**

- `squadA.md` (frontmatter `paths:` + body "Squad A Territory") claims Squad A owns: `overrides/app/pages/home/`, `product-detail/`, `product-list/`, `cart/`, `checkout/`, `checkout-one-click/`, `confirmation/`, plus `header/`, `footer/`, `drawer-menu/`, `list-menu/` (flagged inside the file itself as shared Tier 2 — "coordinate with Squad B"), `sf-payments-express*`, `multiship/`, `bonus-product-view-modal/`, and hooks `use-checkout-auto-select`, `use-multiship`, `use-pickup-shipment`, `use-sf-payments`.
- `squadB.md` claims Squad B owns only `search/`, `account/`, `store-locator/` + hooks `use-product-view-modal`, `use-derived-product`, `use-variant`, `use-wish-list` (future: promotions, Zimmerse, SEO/analytics). It explicitly states: *"`product-detail/` and `product-list/` are Squad A territory."*
- `.docs/memory/sprintScope.md` agrees with this model (Squad A: Homepage, PDP, PLP, Cart, Checkout, Order Management, Payments, Returns; Squad B: Search, Promotions, Store Locator, Zimmerse, SEO).

**But four other real, load-bearing sources say the opposite for Home/PDP/PLP** (while agreeing cart/checkout = A and search/account = B):
- Root `CODEOWNERS` (Tier 3 section) assigns `overrides/app/pages/home/`, `product-detail/`, `product-list/`, `account/`, `wishlist/`, `store-locator/`, `search/` to `@ZimmermannAU/pwa-squad-b`, and only `cart/`, `checkout/` (+ its 4 hooks) to `@ZimmermannAU/pwa-squad-a`.
- The **auto-generated** `.claude/registry/pages.md` (built by `scripts/generateRegistry.mjs`, not hand-opinion) tags `Home`, `ProductDetail`, `ProductList`, `Account`, `StoreLocator` as Squad **B**, and `Cart`, `Checkout`, `CheckoutOneClick`, `Confirmation` as Squad **A**.
- `.claude/rules/protectedFiles.md`'s Tier 2 split reinforces the same model: "Shared Product Components" (`product-tile/`, `product-item/`, `display-price/`, `image-gallery/`, `swatch-group/`, `recommended-products/`) are **Squad B**-owned; "Shared Commerce Components" (`order-summary/`, `promo-code/`, `pickup-or-delivery/`) are **Squad A**-owned — i.e., B = product/discovery domain, A = commerce/checkout domain, which only makes sense if B also owns PDP/PLP.
- Three skills state the CODEOWNERS model explicitly: `.claude/skills/onboarding/SKILL.md` ("Squad B: Homepage, PDP, PLP, search, account, Brochureware Content"), `.claude/skills/feature-spec/SKILL.md` and `.claude/skills/qa-generate/SKILL.md` (both: "B: PDP/PLP/search/account").

**Practical impact:** `audit-tier` and `scope-check` (both `.claude/skills/`) explicitly say to consult `squadA.md`/`squadB.md` for Tier-3 ownership — so today they would tell a developer that Home/PDP/PLP are Squad A's when CODEOWNERS, the registry, and 3 other skills say Squad B. This needs reconciling before the playbook cites either model as ground truth; I'd flag it to Marcel rather than silently pick one side.

Tier-2 "Owner" tags in `protectedFiles.md` are otherwise fully consistent with `CODEOWNERS`'s real GitHub teams (`@ZimmermannAU/tier-1-approvers`, `@ZimmermannAU/tier-2-approvers`, `@ZimmermannAU/pwa-squad-a`, `@ZimmermannAU/pwa-squad-b`) — e.g. Global Shell = both squads + both approver tiers; Theme Component Styles / Translations fall back to the generic approver teams because no dedicated UI-Designer/Integration-Partner GitHub team exists yet (noted inline in CODEOWNERS).

---

### 2. All 14 skills — one-liners + playbook mapping

| Skill | What it actually does |
|---|---|
| `audit-tier` | Given a path, reports its tier (1–4), owner, and import blast-radius via a grep count; tells you who to notify. |
| `code-quality` | Read-only audit of changed/specified files against `conventions.md` (naming, imports, TS coverage, test/story existence) via 4 parallel sub-agents; outputs a 🔴/🟡/🔵 report. |
| `contentful-drift-check` | Read-only diff between a component's TS props and its paired `*ContentfulDefinition.ts` file; reports added/removed/mismatched props. |
| `contentful-register-component` | Reads a component's props, generates a `*ContentfulDefinition.ts` mapping each prop to a Contentful variable type, wires it into the `defineComponents` registry. |
| `feature-spec` | Turns a feature request into a scoped spec: one-question-at-a-time clarification → 3 parallel research agents (registry scan, pattern scan, upstream check) → sprint check → spec with file list, tier flags, and a ready-to-paste Claude Code prompt. |
| `generate-changelog` | Builds a 4-audience changelog (dev/QA/product/GitHub Release) from conventional commits + upstream baseline; writes to `docs/releases/` (path currently doesn't exist — see §6/8 below). |
| `new-component` | Scaffolds `overrides/app/components/<name>/index.tsx` + paired `.stories.tsx` (+ optional `.test.ts`), TypeScript/Chakra, per `conventions.md`. |
| `onboarding` | Interactive first-day walkthrough: role/squad question → mechanical setup checks (git hooks, node version, branch) → role-specific rules orientation → first task. |
| `pr-checklist` | Runs `/code-quality` on `git diff --name-only develop`, classifies each changed file by tier/owner, generates a copy-paste PR description + test checklist. |
| `project-init` | One-time setup: runs `scripts/projectInitCheck.sh`, auto-fixes what it can, asks one question at a time for the rest (Jira prefix, BrowserStack, secrets, Zephyr, LHCI, MuleSoft contract endpoint), writes status back to a **Confluence** checklist page (not a repo file). |
| `qa-generate` | Two-step human-gated E2E generation: Jira story → Gherkin `.feature` file → **stop, wait for Lead QA sign-off** → only then generate the Playwright spec. |
| `scope-check` | Reviews a *proposed* Claude Code prompt before you run it: classifies every file it would likely touch by tier, verdicts SAFE/RISKY/BLOCKED, rewrites risky prompts. |
| `session-start` | Mandatory session ritual: confirm branch safety → read `projectState.md`/`sprintScope.md`/`feedback.md`/`upstreamBaseline.md`/`.claude/session-notes.md` in parallel → run `scripts/healthCheckAll.sh` → state position → wait for confirmation. |
| `upstream-sync-review` | Reviews `@salesforce/retail-react-app` release notes against `upstreamBaseline.md`, maps changes to the override surface, recommends BUMP/DEFER/WAIT. |

**Mapping to playbook concepts:**
- **"Planning layer"/gap-hunting** → `feature-spec` is the real, working operationalization — closer to it than anything else in the repo, including its parallel-research-agent pattern.
- **"Story skill" for component scaffolding** → `new-component` (produces `.tsx` + `.stories.tsx`).
- **Terminology collision — flag explicitly:** `qa-generate` also produces "stories," but a completely different sense — a Jira **user story** (`SFCC-142`) becomes a Gherkin `.feature` file, never a Storybook file. `new-component`'s "story" is a `*.stories.tsx` Storybook file for one component. Same word, two unrelated artifacts, two unrelated skills — worth an explicit terminology note in the playbook so "write a story for X" is unambiguous.
- **"Hardening checklist"** → `code-quality` (read-only audit) + `pr-checklist` (tier-aware PR description generator that invokes `code-quality` first).
- **"build-log.md" memory-at-session-start** → `session-start` is the real mechanism, but it's richer than a single file: team-shared `.docs/memory/*.md` (git-tracked) plus a **personal, gitignored** `.claude/session-notes.md` that Claude may write to directly (per-developer carryover notes) — this gitignored file is the closest single analog to an informal "build-log.md," while `.docs/memory/projectState.md` is the closest analog to a formal one.
- **Scaffolding discipline / one-time setup** → `project-init` (repo-wide, Confluence-tracked) + `onboarding` (per-developer).
- **Tier system** → `audit-tier` (inspect one path) + `scope-check` (inspect a whole prompt before running it) — both real and specified in detail, both currently vulnerable to the squad-ownership contradiction in §1.
- **No playbook equivalent at all** (describe, don't compare):
  - `generate-changelog` — 4-audience release notes from conventional commits.
  - `upstream-sync-review` — governs when to bump the upstream PWA Kit dependency; pairs with `.docs/upstreamPolicy.md`'s "bump opportunistically, not on a schedule" policy.
  - `contentful-register-component` / `contentful-drift-check` — the Contentful Studio Experiences component-registration and drift-audit pair (see §5).

---

### 3. Living memory files — `.docs/memory/*.md`

- **`projectState.md`** (16KB, actively maintained, dated 2026-06-25) is the real "current state" doc — phase, per-integration status (mock/live/not-started), what's done/pending, a long "Unresolved Dependencies" list. This is the closest thing to a project-wide build-log, but it's a snapshot document, not an append-only log.
- **`feedback.md`** — **empty**. Contains only its placeholder comment (`*This document is for documenting what has been learned...*`). It does **not** currently implement the playbook's §9.6 "push corrections into the rules layer" loop — it's wired into `session-start`'s reading list but has never been populated.
- **`sprintScope.md`** — real, a dependency-ordered sprint map (Sprint 0–7) Claude checks before referencing later-sprint code. Currently: Sprint 0 (Foundation) in progress.
- **`references.md`** — real but empty (placeholder only; template for credentials/URLs).
- **`upstreamBaseline.md`** — real and populated: pinned at `@salesforce/retail-react-app@10.0.0`, "Reviewed up to" tracking tied to `.github/workflows/upstream-release-watch.yml`.
- **The actual §9.6-style mechanism is elsewhere:** `.claude/hooks/session-reflect.sh` (a **Stop hook**, wired in `.claude/settings.json`) fires at the end of every session with uncommitted changes and forces Claude to write a dated proposal file to `.docs/agents-proposals/` covering candidate edits to `AGENTS.md`, `.docs/memory/*`, `.claude/rules/*`, PRDs, etc. — explicitly blocking Claude from editing those files directly ("Tier 1 / human-owned"). **This directly contradicts `session-start`'s own instructions**, which tell Claude to "populate [a memory file] the moment you learn something that belongs there" as a direct-write operation, and it also contradicts `frozenFiles.md`, whose Tier-1 Governance list does *not* include `.docs/memory/*` or `.docs/prd/*` at all. In practice `projectState.md` is clearly being edited directly and substantively (rich content, real dated entries), so the Stop-hook's blanket "never edit directly" framing appears to be a newer/stricter rule not yet reconciled with the older direct-write guidance. Worth flagging to Marcel as a real internal inconsistency in the governance layer, not just a documentation gap.

---

### 4. `.docs/planning/sharedAiBrainBrief.md` — HIGH PRIORITY, read in full

This is a detailed Sprint-0 implementation brief (Tim Lavelle, Accenture Song, May 2026) for a **"Shared Brain"**: Confluence pages (labeled `architecture-decision`/`scope-boundary`/`regional-rule`/`open-item`/`meeting-outcome`) → ingestion → pgvector-on-Postgres embeddings → an Express RAG API → an MCP server exposing `query_knowledge` → a `.claude/skills/knowledge.md` `/knowledge` skill for Claude Code, plus a daily auto-generated `TEAM-KNOWLEDGE-SUMMARY.md` uploaded to Claude.ai for non-developers. It explicitly says "add this alongside the existing 13 skills."

**Verified: not built.** No `shared-brain/` directory exists anywhere in the repo. No `.claude/skills/knowledge/` (the 14 skills that do exist match exactly the list given, no 15th). No pgvector/Postgres/embeddings references anywhere else in the repo.

**What *is* real and adjacent:** root `.mcp.json` configures a generic, off-the-shelf **`mcp-atlassian`** MCP server (Jira + Confluence REST, via `uvx mcp-atlassian`, env vars `JIRA_URL`/`JIRA_API_TOKEN`/`CONFLUENCE_URL`/`CONFLUENCE_API_TOKEN`). This is what actually backs the `confluence_get_page`/`confluence_update_page` tool calls referenced in `.claude/skills/project-init/SKILL.md`. It gives Claude Code direct Confluence/Jira read/write, but with **none** of the brief's RAG/semantic-search/conflict-detection/Claude.ai-summary-sync machinery — no vector DB, no ingestion pipeline, no automatic conflict flagging.

**Conclusion for the rewrite:** treat `sharedAiBrainBrief.md` as an aspirational Sprint-0 proposal that was superseded by a much simpler, real solution (direct Atlassian MCP passthrough). Don't cite it as "the planning layer" — cite `feature-spec` (§2) for the AI-planning-layer role, and `.mcp.json`'s `mcp-atlassian` server for the Confluence-connectivity role.

---

### 5. Real component registry — found, and it's better than the playbook's imagined one

`.claude/registry/` contains **five** auto-generated files: `components.md`, `hooks.md`, `pages.md`, `routes.md`, `utils.md` — generated by `node scripts/generateRegistry.mjs` (confirmed real script), refreshed via a `PostToolUse` hook (`.claude/hooks/registryUpdate.sh`, confirmed to exist, wired in `.claude/settings.json`) and read by `feature-spec`/`generate-changelog` when present.

I read `components.md` and `pages.md` in full. Each row has: name, **Origin** (Base/Override/Custom), path, props signature, **Tier**, **Squad**, consumer count, last-touched date, and a description scraped from JSDoc. This directly and concretely answers your §9.4 question: **yes**, a real component-registry.md-equivalent exists, is auto-maintained (not hand-curated), and covers components + hooks + pages + routes + utils, not just components. Separately, `contentful-register-component`/`contentful-drift-check` (§2) serve the narrower Contentful-Studio-definition-sync role you asked about — the two mechanisms are complementary, not the same thing: the registry tracks *all* code-level components; the Contentful skills track only the subset registered with Contentful Studio.

---

### 6. Prompt templates — `.docs/prompts/*.md`

All three are genuine instances of the playbook's §9.5 "build prompt pattern": long, explicit, file-by-file Claude Code prompts meant to be pasted wholesale, each now carrying a `> Status — done. Kept for traceability.` banner listing the artifacts it produced.

**The code/config artifacts they claim are real — verified:**
`.github/workflows/digital-sit.yml`, `playwright.config.js`, `lighthouserc.js`, `.browserstack.yml`, `config/sit.js`, and `package.json` scripts `test:sit`/`test:contracts`/`push:sit`/`activate:sit`/`sync:contentful` all exist exactly as claimed. `e2e/` exists with the described structure (`features/`, `tests/zimm/`, `support/pages/`, `support/helpers/`, `fixtures/`).

**But the documentation artifacts they claim are real — all missing.** Every path under a bare `docs/` (not `.docs/`) — `docs/ciCd/branchProtection.md`, `docs/ciCd/workflowMap.md`, `docs/onboarding/sitQualityGates.md`, `docs/onboarding/branchingGuide.md`, `docs/environments/sit.md`, `docs/environments/topology.md`, `docs/qa/README.md`, `docs/releases/` (also `generate-changelog`'s own output target) — **the `docs/` directory does not exist in this repo at all.** Likely explanation: `AGENTS.md`'s footer says developer onboarding "now lives on Confluence... not loaded into Claude's context," implying a deliberate migration away from local `docs/*.md` that the prompt files' status banners were never updated to reflect. Either way, any playbook citation of those `docs/...` paths is currently a dead link.

**Also found: `e2e/` is 100% JavaScript, not TypeScript** (`BasePage.js`, `CheckoutPage.js`, `ProductPage.js`, `auth.js`, `site.js`, `customers.js`, `products.js`, `orders.js`, `SFCC-000_guest-checkout.p0.spec.js` — 0 `.ts` files, 10 `.js` files) — this contradicts `.claude/skills/qa-generate/SKILL.md`'s explicit rule ("Files are TypeScript (`.spec.ts`) — the TS-only convention applies to E2E too") and `.claude/rules/testing.md`'s Playwright examples (which show `.ts`). AGENTS.md's Hard Rule strictly scopes TS-only to `overrides/`, so this isn't a Hard Rule violation, but it is a real gap between a skill's stated rule and the actual scaffold.

---

### 7. Open items — `.docs/temp/openItems.md`

Yes, this matches the playbook's "keep an open-items list visible" idea closely — 40 numbered items across (nominally) 18 integrations, each with an owner and blocking status, e.g. "Omneo: all 3 items are hard blockers, no Omneo-issued identifiers currently in Accenture's possession." It's a real, well-maintained, single-file open-items register — see §8 for a count discrepancy inside this same file.

---

### 8. Integrations reality check — the playbook's "14 integrations, four connector patterns" claim does not hold up

I read all 6 `.docs/vendor/*.md` and all 19 `.docs/temp/integration/*.md` files (18 numbered + `index.md`). Actual counts, from multiple independent sources, all disagreeing with "14":

- `.docs/temp/integration/index.md` — explicitly indexes **18** PWA-layer systems (numbered 1–18: SFCC, Contentful, MuleSoft, Omneo, GiveX, Booxi, Adyen, Global-e, Google Maps, reCAPTCHA, Narvar, Didomi, GTM, Inside Chat, Optimizely, Crazy Egg, Measmerize, Vimeo), explicitly scoped to *browser-direct + MRT-proxied only*.
- `.docs/temp/openItems.md` **contradicts itself**: its own intro prose says "the fifteen external integrations in scope," but its own table has 18 rows and its own total line reads "**Total: 40 items across 18 integrations.**" "Fifteen" is simply wrong per the file's own table.
- `.docs/memory/projectState.md`'s "Integrations" status table lists **18** rows (SFCC, Contentful, Global-e, Didomi, Omneo, Emarsys, MuleSoft, NewStore OMS, AP21, Adyen, Narvar, Google Maps, Avalara, GiveX, Inside Chat, Transperfect, Google Business API, Feedonomics).
- `.docs/architecture.md`'s full Integration Map (which also includes server-to-server/out-of-band systems the PWA-layer docs explicitly exclude — Avalara, Transperfect, Zendesk, Shippit/Ordoro, Google Business API, Feedonomics, GDPR cartridge, Emarsys, NewStore OMS, AP21) lists **~28** systems.
- `.docs/vendor/*.md` covers only 5 actual vendors in depth (Didomi, GiveX, Measmerize, MuleSoft, Optimizely) — a small subset, not a complete count.

**"14" appears nowhere.** Depending on which scope you mean, the real number is 18 (PWA-layer, per the integration-docs index and projectState.md) or ~28 (everything, per architecture.md's full map) — recommend the rewrite cite "18 PWA-layer integrations (see `.docs/temp/integration/index.md`)" and drop "14" entirely.

**"Four connector patterns routing through MuleSoft" is unverifiable/likely invented.** No document states a specific count of MuleSoft connector patterns. `.docs/architecture.md`'s "Boundary key" defines 7 general boundary categories (PWA-direct, MRT-mediated, SFCC OOTB, SFCC cartridge, SFCC→MuleSoft, Browser handoff, Out-of-band), and the MuleSoft-specific routing shape is described per-integration and is genuinely heterogeneous — e.g. GiveX alone uses three distinct MuleSoft-involving legs (SCAPI/SFCC→NewStore-adapter→GiveX for validate/redeem/refund; SCAPI/SFCC→MuleSoft→NewStore→GiveX for issuance; MRT→MuleSoft→GiveX for balance check), while `03-mulesoft.md` documents exactly 2 confirmed PWA-direct endpoint groups (orders/returns via `magento-exp-api`; Find In Store) plus several ⏳-pending ones. There is no "four pattern" taxonomy anywhere I read — recommend dropping this claim unless it traces to the solution deck the playbook author had separately (which isn't in this repo).

---

### 9. `.docs/agents-proposals/README.md`

One line: *"Agent-drafted documentation proposals. Stop-hook output. Review and apply manually — never auto-merge."* The directory contains only this README (no proposal files present in this checkout). This is **not** a roadmap of planned future agent work — it's the human-facing inbox description for the real mechanism I traced in §3: `.claude/hooks/session-reflect.sh`, a Stop hook that, at the end of any session with uncommitted changes, forces Claude to draft a single timestamped proposal file here (`{timestamp}-{branch}.md`) covering candidate updates to `AGENTS.md`/`.docs/memory/*`/`.claude/rules/*`/PRDs — never editing those directly. For a "multiply the team" narrative, this is a real, working (if narrow) instance of AI-drafted-but-human-gated documentation upkeep — worth describing precisely as that, not over-selling it as a broader agent-roadmap.

---

### 10. Branch/release/CI-CD workflow — one paragraph

Six-tier topology (`Local → Dev → SIT (parallel) → Stage → UAT → Prod`, per `.docs/architecture.md` §Environments and `.docs/temp/tsd-architecture.md`), with `feature/*` → `develop` → `release/v*.*.*` → `main` as the branch chain (plus `hotfix/*` from `main`, back-merged per `.docs/releaseBranchesRules.md`). NewStore's OMS SIT runs as a genuinely parallel, non-blocking lane that only converges with Digital at the Stage tier (Jira-booked, dual sign-off required) — confirming the playbook's "Digital SIT; NewStore SIT" framing is directionally correct. Additional real workflows beyond what any doc set fully narrates: `deploy-dev.yml`, `deploy-sit.yml`, `deploy-stg.yml`, `deploy-uat.yml`, `deploy-prod.yml` (one per tier), `protected-file-guard.yml` (20KB — the non-blocking Tier-1 PR warning bot described in `AGENTS.md`'s "Tier 1 Approval" section), `upstream-release-watch.yml`, and `weekly-agents.yml` (see below).

1. **Squad ownership contradiction** (§1) — `squadA.md`/`squadB.md`/`sprintScope.md` vs. `CODEOWNERS`/`.claude/registry/pages.md`/`onboarding`/`feature-spec`/`qa-generate` disagree on who owns Home/PDP/PLP. Cart/checkout=A and search/account=B are undisputed; Home/PDP/PLP is the live fault line.

3. **"Four connector patterns through MuleSoft"** — unverifiable, no doc states this; the real pattern is heterogeneous per-integration (§8).
4. **`docs/` paths in the three prompt templates** (§6) — all dead; the directory doesn't exist. The underlying CI/CD code they describe is real; the documentation half of their "done" claims is not.
5. **`qa-generate` vs. `new-component` "story"** (§2) — same word, two unrelated artifact types (Jira story→Gherkin feature vs. Storybook story file). Flag explicitly if the playbook uses "story" unqualified.
6. **`e2e/` is JavaScript, not TypeScript** (§6) — contradicts `qa-generate`'s and `testing.md`'s stated TS-only rule for E2E.

Here's what the research surfaced, and the plan for the playbook.

## What we learned

**The playbook's own design principle** (§0): sections 1–9 stay pure "training methodology," and all Zimmermann-specific mapping is quarantined to §16 ("Bridge to Zimmermann"), which explicitly labels itself an *unconfirmed hypothesis from a solution deck* — not from the training, not from the repo. That's exactly the gap now closed.

**Two mechanical bugs**, independent of the research:
- §0 and §6 both cross-reference "section 10" for the bridge — it's actually §16 now (stale renumbering).
- §4 asserts "you already do this" about a committed account-level anti-agreeableness instructions file. manndotfiles research found no such file exists anywhere — the real analogs are tool config (`effortLevel: "high"`, curated plugins like `superpowers`/`pr-review-toolkit` that push back on rubber-stamping). The claim overclaims a fact, inside a section meant to stay training-generic.

**Real, corrected facts for §16** (full detail in `[[project-zimmermann-pwa]]` memory):
- "14 integrations, four MuleSoft connector patterns" is wrong under every source — real count is 18 PWA-layer (~28 including server-to-server); no doc supports a "four patterns" figure.
- `sharedAiBrainBrief.md`'s RAG/pgvector knowledge base was never built — real Confluence/Jira access is a plain `mcp-atlassian` MCP server.
- `feedback.md` (the imagined "corrections loop") is empty — the real mechanism is a Stop hook drafting proposals to `.docs/agents-proposals/` for human review.
- A live, unresolved **squad-ownership contradiction**: `squadA.md`/`squadB.md`/`sprintScope.md` say Squad A owns Home/PDP/PLP; CODEOWNERS + the auto-generated registry + 3 skills say Squad B does. This is a perfect real worked example of the exact gap-hunting the playbook preaches.
- Real capabilities the playbook never mentions: an auto-generated component/hook/page/route registry (richer than the playbook's imagined `component-registry.md`), 5 automation hooks, CodeRabbit as a second AI reviewer, a misleadingly-named `weekly-agents.yml` (no AI agent involved).
- A "story" terminology collision: component-build story (playbook's sense) vs. Storybook `.stories.tsx` vs. Jira/Gherkin QA story — three different things, same word.

## Proposed edits

1. Fix the two stale "section 10" → "section 16" refs (§0, §6).
2. Soften §4's overclaim — replace the specific "you already do this" file-claim with an accurate, brief pointer to §16.
3. Rewrite §16 in place, restructured into subsections:
   - **16.1** Real artifact mapping table (methodology concept → verified repo path), replacing the speculative stack-swap table.
   - **16.2** Corrections to prior assumptions (integrations count, connector patterns, shared-brain-brief, feedback.md) — stated as corrections, not hedged hypotheses, since these are now verified.
   - **16.3** Real capabilities not covered above (registry, hooks, CodeRabbit, weekly-agents, Cursor/VS Code sync) — things a Lead should know exist.
   - **16.4** A live worked example: the squad-ownership contradiction, framed as "your first gap-hunt" — flagged, not resolved (that's Marcel's call with the actual leads, not mine).
   - **16.5** Updated honest close.
4. Update §16's opening framing from "unconfirmed hypothesis" to "verified against the real repo on 2026-07-09; open items flagged below."

I won't touch sections 1–9's actual methodology content — that's deliberately training-pure per the doc's own rule, and nothing in the research contradicts it.

Want me to go ahead and write this, or adjust scope first (e.g., trim §16.3, or handle the squad-ownership conflict differently)?

| Training (TelcoNow) | Zimmermann — verified |
|---|---|

| `create-next-app` scaffold | PWA Kit generator — same rule: don't run it by hand, let Claude Code build from the brief |
| NextAuth | SFCC / SLAS auth, handled in `overrides/app/ssr/slasTokens.ts` (Tier 1) — the React idioms don't map, learn the PWA Kit way |
| Contentful (training's headless CMS) | Genuinely in scope. Two real, complementary mechanisms handle it: `.claude/skills/contentful-register-component` generates a component's Contentful Studio definition; `.claude/skills/contentful-drift-check` audits an existing definition against current props. Run drift-check before assuming a definition is current. |
| Tailwind tokens | Chakra UI props first, tokens in `overrides/app/theme/foundation/` (Tier 1, UI-designer owned) |
| `build-log.md` (imagined) | No single file. Team-shared state lives in `.docs/memory/projectState.md` (formal snapshot) plus a personal, gitignored `.claude/session-notes.md` (informal per-developer carryover). Both are read by the `/session-start` skill at the top of every session — run it. |
| `component-registry.md` (imagined) | **Better than imagined.** `.claude/registry/{components,hooks,pages,routes,utils}.md` — auto-generated by `scripts/generateRegistry.mjs`, refreshed on every file write by a hook. Not hand-curated, so it can't go stale from someone forgetting to update it. |
| "Story skill" (component scaffold) | `.claude/skills/new-component` — scaffolds `index.tsx` + `index.stories.tsx` (+ a test if logic-heavy) per `conventions.md`. **Terminology warning:** don't say "story" unqualified to the squad. `new-component`'s story is a Storybook file. `.claude/skills/qa-generate`'s story is a Jira user story becoming a Gherkin `.feature` file. Same word, two unrelated artifacts — be explicit about which one you mean. |
| Two-reviewer gap-hunt | `.claude/skills/feature-spec` is the real, working planning-layer skill — one-question-at-a-time clarification, then parallel research agents against the registry/patterns/upstream, then a scoped spec with a ready-to-paste Claude Code prompt. This is closer to the training's ideal than the training's own workflow was. |
| Hardening checklist | `.claude/skills/code-quality` (read-only audit against `conventions.md`) and `.claude/skills/pr-checklist` (runs code-quality, then classifies every changed file by tier/owner into a PR description). Run both before opening a PR, not just before calling something "done" in your head. |
| The "corrections → rules layer" loop (§9.6) | Partially automated, not manual-only as the training assumed: a Stop hook (`.claude/hooks/session-reflect.sh`) fires at the end of any session with uncommitted changes and drafts a dated proposal into `.docs/agents-proposals/` covering candidate edits to `AGENTS.md` / `.docs/memory/*` / `.claude/rules/*`. It never auto-merges — you still review and apply by hand. `.docs/memory/feedback.md` itself is currently empty; the hook is the active loop, not that file. |

**Still accurate, now with real names attached:** the rules layer as a **shared, two-squad contract** (not personal memory) remains arguably your single highest-leverage responsibility as FE Lead — this is the scale gap from §0. The regroup culture (§14) is still your cross-squad review cadence, run on your sprint/PI rhythm. Descope-never-cut, the 20-min rule, and deploy-first still directly protect margin on a fixed-price engagement. And the CI-CD gates are real and confirmed: `qa.yml` (Vitest + Storybook a11y, every PR into `develop`/`release/**`) and `digital-sit.yml` — the composite "Digital SIT Gate" (Playwright P0 + bundle-size + Lighthouse CI) on `release/**`. NewStore's OMS SIT runs as a genuinely parallel, non-blocking lane that only converges with Digital at the Stage tier — the original "Digital SIT; NewStore SIT" framing was directionally right; now you have the actual workflow files to point to.

### 16.2 Corrections — claims that didn't hold up

- **"14 integrations, four connector patterns routing through MuleSoft" — wrong, drop it.** No document in the repo supports either number. The real count is **18 PWA-layer integrations** (`.docs/temp/integration/index.md`, confirmed by `.docs/memory/projectState.md`'s status table), or **~28** including server-to-server/out-of-band systems (`.docs/architecture.md`'s full integration map — Avalara, Transperfect, Zendesk, Feedonomics, and others). Even `.docs/temp/openItems.md` contradicts itself — its prose says "fifteen," its own table and total line say 18. Cite "18 PWA-layer integrations" and drop the connector-pattern count entirely; the real MuleSoft routing is heterogeneous per integration (GiveX alone uses three different MuleSoft-involving paths depending on validate/redeem/issue/balance).
- **The "shared AI brain" isn't real — don't cite it as infrastructure.** `.docs/planning/sharedAiBrainBrief.md` proposes a pgvector/RAG knowledge base with its own MCP server and a `/knowledge` skill. It was never built — no fifteenth skill, no vector DB, nothing. What *is* real and does the Confluence/Jira-connectivity job it was reaching for: a plain `mcp-atlassian` MCP server, configured in root `.mcp.json`, giving Claude Code direct Jira/Confluence read/write with none of the semantic-search ambition. Don't oversell the aspiration to the squad as if it shipped.
- **The account-level instructions baseline from §4 doesn't exist as a file yet.** There is no committed prose instructions document anywhere in `manndotfiles` or elsewhere on this machine — verified directly. What you actually have is *tool configuration*: `claude/settings.seed.json` sets a global `effortLevel: "high"` dial, and your curated plugin list (`superpowers`, `code-review`, `pr-review-toolkit`) pulls in skills that already push back on rubber-stamping by design (e.g. `superpowers:receiving-code-review` explicitly requires "technical rigor and verification, not performative agreement"). 1	# The Frontend Development Lead Playbook
2	### Zimmermann Commerce Migration · How to be the FE Lead as both IC and Senior/Lead
3	
4	*Distilled from the Manila AI Engineering Training Week (June 2026, facilitated by Tim Lavelle). This is your operating manual, not a summary of the week.*
5	
6	---
7	
8	## 0. How to use this document
9	
10	This is the standard you hold yourself and your squad to. Read it once end-to-end, then treat it as a lookup — every section is written so you can jump to it mid-delivery.
11	
12	**Source and provenance — read this once so you never confuse the two layers:**
13	
14	- Everything in sections 1–9 is grounded in the **Manila training**. The training vehicle was a *TelcoNow B2C portal* on **Next.js 14 · TypeScript · Tailwind · Contentful**. That is what was actually taught.
15	- The training's *methodology* is deliberately stack-agnostic. Its closing thesis: **"The discipline transfers. The specific tools won't."** That is why it maps onto Zimmermann at all.
16	- Anything about **SFCC / PWA Kit / MRT / the two squads / RACI / CI-CD gates / integrations** is **me bridging to your project** from separate context (the solution deck and project setup). It is labeled as a bridge in **section 16**, which has since been verified against the real repo (2026-07-09) — corrections and open items are called out there, not silently folded in here. Don't cite section 16 as training content; it still isn't.
17	
18	**The three gaps you carry into this role — stated plainly, because pretending they aren't there is how leads fail:**
19	
20	1. **Framework gap.** You're Angular-primary. The training and the project are React (Next in training, PWA Kit in project). The *habits* below transfer cleanly. The *code idioms* do not. Build PWA Kit / React fluency as a separate, explicit track — don't let the transferable methodology fool you into thinking the framework transfers with it.
21	2. **Scale gap.** The training taught *solo* builds. You lead *shared-codebase, two-squad* delivery. Every "memory for future-you" artifact below has to be re-read as "contract for the whole team." Section 10 makes that jump concrete.
22	3. **Leadership gap.** You are stepping up into the lead seat. The IC craft you already have. The lead craft — running review culture, protecting quality under pressure, multiplying yourself — is the part this document is really for.
23	
24	---
25	
26	## 1. The one principle everything hangs on
27	
28	> **The quality ceiling is set by the human, not the AI.**
29	
30	Claude will match the quality of what you give it. Give it a vague plan, you get plausible garbage that costs hours to unwind. Give it a tight contract, sharp stories, and enforced rules, and you get output you'd have been proud to write yourself. This is true today and it will be true in two years when the tools have changed names.
31	
32	Two corollaries the training hammered:
33	
34	- **Claude is not autocomplete.** It's a co-engineer with memory and constraints — but the memory and the constraints are *things you supply*. It has no standards of its own. You are the standard.
35	- **Claude makes your assumptions visible faster.** That's the actual value. Not that it writes code — that it exposes the gap in your thinking in ten minutes instead of on Thursday night. Treat every gap it surfaces as a gift, not an insult.
36	
37	Everything else is mechanics in service of this.
38	
39	---
40	
41	## 2. The dual mandate
42	
43	You wear two hats *at the same time*, not in alternation. The failure mode is collapsing into one:
44	
45	- **Collapse into IC** → you ship your own components beautifully and the squad drifts, the rules layer rots, and nobody but you knows what "done" means.
46	- **Collapse into Lead** → you run great regroups and review everyone's work but haven't touched the codebase in three weeks, so your technical judgment goes stale and your reviews become vibes.
47	
48	Hold both. Here is the shift in each hat — same activity, two altitudes:
49	
50	| Dimension | As Individual Contributor | As Senior / Lead |
51	|---|---|---|
52	| **Think** | Get *this* component right — states, edges, what Claude will get wrong before it does. | Get the *system* right — will this decision collide with the other squad, the integration seams, go-live? |
53	| **Ask** | "What does this story not tell Claude Code?" | "What does our *rules layer* not tell any developer or any Claude instance on this project?" |
54	| **Communicate** | Precise AC, precise commit, precise "here's what Claude got wrong and why." | Frame reviews as work-not-person, translate across dev/BA/tester/SA, make commitments checkable. |
55	| **Decide** | Monolith or split *your* file, hook or component for *this* value — and defend it. | Set the *convention* the squad decides by, so nobody re-litigates it per component. |
56	| **Review** | Read your own output against the story before you commit. | Run the loop that makes *everyone's* output legible, and catch drift across the codebase. |
57	| **Think beyond** | The next component, the next state, the downstream effect of a data-shape choice. | What happens when you're *not in the room*. The team you're growing. Maintainability in 2027. |
58	| **Protect** | Your commit doesn't introduce a hardcoded hex or an `any`. | The *whole codebase's* quality bar holds under deadline pressure — including when it's inconvenient. |
59	| **Multiply** | You get faster and cleaner. | The room gets faster and cleaner *because of how you work*. You are the capability anchor. |
60	
61	The training's own closing line for the cohort — *"This group is the capability anchor; the expectation is that what you learned reaches the people who weren't in this room"* — is a job description for the Lead hat. Internalize it.
62	
63	---
64	
65	## 3. Tooling model: two tools, two mindsets, one handoff
66	
67	The single most consequential distinction in the whole week:
68	
69	- **Claude.ai = the planning partner.** It explores, suggests, asks questions, thinks out loud with you. Use it to *decide*.
70	- **Claude Code = the engineering colleague in your terminal.** It reads files, writes code, runs commands. Critically: **it does not ask what you meant — it infers and proceeds.** Use it to *build*.
71	
72	**The handoff rule:** move from Claude.ai to Claude Code only *when you trust your plan enough to stop editing it and start building from it.* Not before.
73	
74	**The most common mistake — and it will tempt your whole squad:** moving to Claude Code too early because you're excited to build. Then Claude Code starts inventing things to fill the gaps you left, and by mid-sprint you're fighting the tool instead of directing it.
75	
76	- *IC discipline:* Don't open Claude Code on a story you haven't hardened. If you're still discovering questions, you're still in Claude.ai.
77	- *Lead discipline:* Watch for the squad jumping to build early. "Is your plan ready for that?" is the question you ask before anyone scaffolds. The moment Claude Code reads a plan and finds the gaps is the most important moment — make the squad *curious* about it, not defensive.
78	
79	---
80	
81	## 4. Defeating agreeableness — the skill the whole week is built on
82	
83	**Claude is optimised to be helpful, which means optimised to agree.** Left to its defaults it will praise a plan that produces unusable output. Agreeable defaults produce unchallenged assumptions, and unchallenged assumptions cost hours of rework on a real, fixed-price engagement.
84	
85	You break the default deliberately. Four techniques, each producing meaningfully different output. These are your reusable prompts — adapt the wording, keep the intent:
86	
87	1. **Role framing** — *"Act as a senior engineer whose job is to find flaws in plans before they reach production. Be direct. Don't soften criticism."*
88	2. **Steelman** — *"What is the strongest argument against this approach? What would go wrong if we built this exactly as described?"*
89	3. **Critique-first** — *"Before telling me what's good about this, list every weakness, gap, or assumption you're making. Weaknesses first, always."*
90	4. **Constraint injection** — *"Assume this goes to production at scale. Assume a QA engineer rejects it if there are no tests. Assume a designer rejects it if there are hardcoded values. Now review it."*
91	
92	**Set a persistent baseline at the account level.** Account instructions change Claude's default behaviour across *every* conversation. The working style this session describes — "lead with the point, flag the trade-off mid-response, challenge like a senior reviewing a PR" — is the target. What you actually have today is a *tool-configuration* baseline, not a committed instructions file: a global effort dial and a curated plugin list that already push back on rubber-stamping (see §16.2). That's a real approximation, but don't assume the gap is already closed — closing it deliberately means writing the actual instructions, not just configuring the tool around the edges.
93	
94	- *IC discipline:* Never accept the first response on anything that matters. If Claude found nothing wrong with your plan, that's a signal to apply technique 1 or 2, not a signal you're done.
95	- *Lead discipline:* Make anti-agreeableness a *team norm*, not your private trick. A squad that accepts Claude's first answer wholesale will produce a codebase full of unexamined assumptions. Teach the four techniques. Put them in the shared rules. Ask in regroup: *"What did Claude agree with that it shouldn't have?"*
96	
97	---
98	
99	## 5. Context and thread hygiene
100	
101	Long conversations degrade output. Every message carries the full history; on a long thread the relevant signal gets buried in noise and quality quietly drops.
102	
103	The rules:
104	
105	- **New conversation when the topic shifts.** Topics bleed across context and pollute each other.
106	- **Name conversations like files, not chat logs.** `checkout-fetch-pattern`, not "SFCC stuff." Treat them as a structured archive you can navigate.
107	- **Aim for 8–10 named, focused threads**, not one 80-message thread called "Zimmermann."
108	- **Claude.ai Projects share context across conversations** — use a Project for planning. **Claude Code uses the repo's rules/context files instead** (`CLAUDE.md` + the `.claude/` layer).
109	
110	- *IC discipline:* One topic per thread. The moment you notice yourself pasting unrelated context to "remind" Claude, you needed a new thread three messages ago.
111	- *Lead discipline:* At team scale, thread hygiene stops being about *your* signal and becomes about *shared* context. What lives in a personal thread is invisible to the squad; what needs to be shared belongs in the Project or the rules layer, not buried in someone's chat history. Decide, as lead, what's personal-thread vs shared-artifact — and make that call explicit so the team isn't guessing.

115	## 6. The planning layer — your codebase's constitution
116	
117	This is where the quality ceiling is actually set. In the training it was a `.claude/` structure; on your project it's the equivalent rules-and-context layer (section 16 maps the names).
118	
119	### `CLAUDE.md` is a contract, not a readme
120	
121	It tells Claude exactly **what to build**, **how to build it**, and **what NOT to do**. Claude Code reads it at the start of *every* session. It is the entry point every prompt begins from.
122	
123	- **Use Claude to *critique* the contract, not rewrite it.** Ask what's wrong; fix one problem at a time. If you let Claude rewrite it wholesale you get a file that reflects Claude's assumptions, not your decisions.
124	- **Each fix should change *structure or specificity*, not wording.** Polishing sentences is procrastination. If your edit didn't change what Claude can or can't do, it wasn't a real edit.
125	
126	### One topic per file — a hard rule
127	
128	If a file covers two things, Claude gets confused about which one applies. So: `build-spec.md`, `solution-architecture.md`, `auth-spec.md`, `design-system.md`, `api-patterns.md`, `component-registry.md` — one concern each. The training's own structure split a `brief/` folder (the *what* and *how*) from a `rules/` layer (the enforceable constraints Claude checks against).
129	
130	**Monolith vs split is a real decision.** Both are defensible *if you can defend it* — but the split is where a serious project lands. A monolithic file and a split set of files produce genuinely *different* Claude Code output. Know why you chose yours.
131	
132	### `build-log.md` is memory, not documentation
133	
134	Claude reads it at the start of every session to know what state the project is in and what's already been done. It is how a fresh Claude Code session — with no memory of yesterday — picks up where you left off.
135	
136	### Define "done" — or Claude Code never stops
137	
138	Claude Code with no stopping condition keeps building components forever. If your file doesn't say what "done" looks like, Claude will invent more work. **Where does your file say what done is?** If it doesn't, that's a bug in the plan, not the tool.
139	
140	- *IC discipline:* Before you build, three questions must be *yes*: does Claude know exactly what to build, exactly how, and exactly what not to do? If any is no, fix it before you open Claude Code.
141	- *Lead discipline:* The planning layer is the highest-leverage thing you own. **This is a system, not a personal note.** A rule that isn't checkable is an aspiration Claude will ignore — police the difference across the whole `rules/` layer. And because two squads read the same files, ambiguity here isn't one dev's rework, it's a fork in the codebase. Owning this well is worth more than any component you'll personally write.

145	## 7. Gap-hunting before the build
146	
147	**Find every gap before Claude Code does. Every gap in your planning files costs time in the build** — and on a fixed-price job, that time comes out of margin.
148	
149	**Use two reviewers with different mindsets, in order:**
150	
151	1. **Claude.ai first** — the conversational reviewer. Prompt it as a senior engineer handing the project to a junior who'll build it with Claude Code: *"Find every place Claude Code would have to make an assumption because I haven't told it what to do. Be specific. Don't be kind."*
152	2. **Claude Code second** — the builder's reviewer. *"Read all files. Do not write code yet. Tell me: every assumption you'd have to make; every instruction that conflicts with another; every topic the files don't cover; check framework versions are current LTS; check the sample code is correct and uses our methodology; any flaws with downstream impact. Reference the file and line for each."*
153	
154	**The contrast between what Claude.ai flags and what Claude Code flags is the lesson.** Claude.ai catches conceptual holes; Claude Code catches build-breaking ones. Whatever gaps remain after both — they're *knowable*, and knowable gaps are the ones you can close.
155	
156	**The distinction that separates real work from theatre:** *"Is that gap fixed now, or did you just acknowledge it?"* Acknowledging a gap in conversation and moving on is the seductive failure. Fixing means the file changed.
157	
158	- *IC discipline:* Run both reviewers on your own stories before you build. "What did Claude just find that I thought was obvious?" is the most useful question you'll ask all day.
159	- *Lead discipline:* Institutionalize the two-reviewer pass as a squad ritual before any sprint. And guard against acknowledge-don't-fix at the team level — in review, don't ask "did Claude flag anything?", ask "show me the file line you changed."

163	## 8. Scaffolding discipline
164	
165	**Do not scaffold by hand.** Running the framework's project generator manually (`create-next-app` in training; the PWA Kit generator on your project) *skips the brief entirely* — Claude Code won't wire up your design tokens, routes, env vars, or folder structure, and you'll spend Wednesday paying for it.
166	
167	Instead: let Claude Code **read the brief and execute every setup step**, as an explicit numbered sequence — configure design tokens, set up fonts, create the folder structure from the architecture file, wire env placeholders, create the build-log with a setup checklist as its first entry. **Confirm each step; list every file created at the end.**
168	
169	- *IC discipline:* After generation, don't trust — verify. Open the token config; missing tokens cause compile errors downstream. A green scaffold checklist exists precisely so this moment is fast and unambiguous.
170	- *Lead discipline:* The scaffold sets conventions the whole squad inherits. Get the folder structure, token config, and env contract right *once*, centrally — every shortcut here is multiplied across every developer who builds on top of it.

174	## 9. The build loop — the core craft
175	
176	This is the part that "makes the methodology different from just prompting." Everything above exists to make this loop clean.
177	
178	### 9.1 Atomic design, bottom-up
179	
180	Build in layers: **layout primitives → atoms → molecules → components.** The lower layers are the foundation; you generate them from the design-system spec *first*, review them carefully, and everything above imports them.
181	
182	### 9.2 The story skill — consistency at scale
183	
184	A **skill is a reusable Claude prompt** that produces consistent, buildable output given a component name. You build one `story-skill` conversation and drive it with a command: `/create-story [ComponentName]`.
185	
186	A good story is **thin — intent and constraints, not implementation detail.** The non-negotiable format:
187	
188	- Follows the story template exactly.
189	- References the *correct* design file and the *correct* data stub (or none, for static components).
190	- **AC describes behaviour, not implementation** — something a tester can verify without asking a developer what it means.
191	- **Always includes happy path + loading-state AC + error-state AC.** Three states, every time.
192	- **Flags anything uncertain rather than inventing it.**
193	
194	**The skill is only as good as its prompt — and the prompt gets better every time you find a gap in its output.** Run it, find what it invented or left vague, refine one thing, run again. The second output is tighter. *That iteration is the lesson* — it's the same feedback loop as section 9.6, applied to your tooling.
195	
196	### 9.3 Generate is 10%. Review is 90%.
197	
198	Generating a component or a story takes a minute. **The work is the review.** A bad story generates a bad component; five minutes reviewing a story now saves an hour tonight.
199	
200	**Hard rule: no one builds from a story they haven't personally read and checked.** Not you, not anyone on the squad.
201	
202	### 9.4 The registry — import, don't reinvent
203	
204	`component-registry.md` lists what exists, where it lives, and its data source. Before building anything: **check the registry and import what's there — do not rebuild atoms inline.** After building: **update the registry.**
205	
206	The test: *"If Claude Code opens this repo tomorrow with no memory of today, does it find a registry that tells it what's already built?"* On a solo project that's a convenience. **On two squads it's the difference between reuse and three developers building three different `StatusBadge`s.**
207	
208	### 9.5 The loop itself
209	
210	> **story → build → review → correct → commit.** One story, one prompt, one review, one commit.
211	
212	The build prompt pattern, every component: *read the registry, read the design-system rules, read this component's story, read the design file — confirm what you read before writing a single line of code — build exactly as specified, import from the registry, don't reinvent.*
213	
214	- *IC discipline:* Run the loop honestly on your own components. When Claude Code does something the story didn't specify, that's a defect in the story — go fix the story (9.6), don't just patch the code.
215	- *Lead discipline:* The loop is what you're teaching and enforcing. In review, verify the loop *ran*: "Did Claude Code read the story before building, or did you just hand it the design file?" A squad that skips the story and prompts from the design file is doing exactly the thing the methodology exists to prevent.
216	
217	### 9.6 The feedback loop that hardens the rules layer
218	
219	The most important habit for long-term quality:
220	
221	> **"Find one place where Claude Code made a decision you didn't specify. What would you add to the AC or the rules to prevent that next time?"**
222	
223	Every correction is data. A correction you make once and forget is a correction you'll make fifty times across the codebase. A correction you *push back into the story template or the rules layer* is made once, forever, for the whole squad. This is how the rules layer becomes real instead of aspirational — and it's pure Lead leverage.

227	## 10. The quality bar and the anti-patterns
228	
229	### The hardening checklist — every component, non-negotiable
230	
231	Run this on every component before it's "done." (Stack names are translated to your project; the *intent* is verbatim from training.)
232	
233	- **Mobile layout at 375px** — actually open dev tools and check.
234	- **Loading state present — a skeleton, not a spinner.**
235	- **Error state present — a proper error component *with retry*.**
236	- **No hardcoded hex values — design tokens only.**
237	- **No TypeScript `any`** — strict mode on. *(This is already your default per your working style — hold the squad to it.)*
238	- **Deployed and resolving — matches local, not just running locally.**
239	- **Registry updated with everything built.**
240	
241	### Anti-patterns to catch on sight
242	
243	- **Over-engineering.** A static banner that should be ~25–35 lines of JSX comes back as 120 — that's Claude over-engineering; simplify it. If a trivial component takes too long to build, the problem is usually the atom layer underneath, not the component.
244	- **Logic in the wrong place.** Derive calculated values (a `percentUsed`, a `daysRemaining`) **in the component, not the hook** — or wherever your `api-patterns` rule specifies. The point isn't the specific rule; it's *consistency* — watch for Claude Code *drifting* from the pattern across components.
245	- **Fetch inside the component.** Data-fetching follows the shared pattern (a hook / service layer), *not* inline in the component.
246	- **UI state vs server state confusion.** A local toggle is local UI state — it does not round-trip to the API. Know which is which and don't let Claude blur them.
247	- **Invented data sources.** A *derived* component (one whose data comes from other components' data) does not get its own stub or its own API call. If Claude invents one, **fix the story, not the code.**
248	- **Rebuilt assets.** Complex SVGs / illustrations get copied from the design file verbatim — don't let Claude "recreate" them from scratch.
249	- **Hardcoded-per-item logic.** Icon or variant selection driven by a `type` enum, not a hardcoded branch per item.
250	
251	- *IC discipline:* Harden your own work to this bar before you'd dream of asking anyone else to.
252	- *Lead discipline:* This checklist is your review rubric and your definition of team-done. The over-engineering and drift checks especially are things *only a senior eye catches* — juniors accept whatever compiles. That catch is a large part of what you're paid for.

256	## 11. Shipping discipline — pragmatism under a fixed-price clock
257	
258	The training's pragmatism is directly relevant to a fixed-price, deadline-bound delivery:
259	
260	- **Deploy first.** A local build that hasn't shipped is invisible — to the review, to the client, to everyone. *"A local build that hasn't shipped is invisible to the regroup."*
261	- **A partial-but-hardened deliverable beats a complete-but-broken one.** *"A deployed page with a loading state beats a perfect local component."* *"A partial portal with hardened components beats a complete portal with broken states."*
262	- **Descope — never cut.** When something runs over: reduce scope (the complex chart becomes a data table — same data, no charting library), commit a loading-skeleton placeholder, and move on. **Never delete the component entirely.** Something honest in place beats a hole.
263	- **The 20-minute rule.** If a fix will take more than ~20 minutes right before a deadline, it's not worth doing before the milestone. Ship what's done and done well; log the rest.
264	- **Compare against the design, side by side.** Design file on one half of the screen, live URL on the other. Divergence you can't see, you can't fix.
265	
266	- *IC discipline:* Make the descope call on your own work early and without ego. Running over at the 80% mark? Stop, commit a clean placeholder, move on.
267	- *Lead discipline:* You own the *triage* across the squad — what gets hardened, what gets descoped, what gets cut for the milestone. Protecting the quality bar under deadline pressure is the specific test of whether you're actually leading or just hoping. Hold the bar when it's inconvenient; that's when it counts.

271	## 12. Cross-cutting dimensions — the "etc."
272	
273	The user asked for the *etc.* explicitly. Here is the full dual-lens reference — the same eleven capabilities, each in both hats. This is the section to reread before a hard week.
274	
275	**Think.**
276	IC — one component deep: states, edges, and *what Claude will get wrong before it does.* Lead — one system wide: does this decision collide with the other squad, the integration seams, the go-live sequence, maintainability in 2027?
277	
278	**Ask.** *(full question bank in section 13)*
279	IC — the questions that expose gaps in *a story*. Lead — the questions that expose gaps in *the rules layer, the conventions, and the team's understanding.*
280	
281	**Communicate.**
282	IC — precise AC, precise commits, precise "here's what Claude got right and what I corrected and why" (specificity over politeness — the *correction* is the more valuable half). Flag uncertainty; never invent. Lead — frame reviews as *work-not-person*; translate across dev/BA/tester/SA; keep the showcase *honest, not polished*; make every commitment specific enough that someone could check it in three months.
283	
284	**Decide.**
285	IC — monolith-or-split for *your* files, hook-or-component for *this* value — and be able to defend it. Lead — set the *convention* so the squad doesn't re-litigate the same decision every component; document it in the rules layer.
286	
287	**Review.**
288	IC — your own output against the story, before commit, honestly. Lead — run the loop that makes *everyone's* work legible; catch pattern-drift across the codebase that no single-component view reveals.
289	
290	**Ship.**
291	IC — deploy your own work, descope early, no ego. Lead — triage what hardens / descopes / cuts across the whole squad against the milestone.
292	
293	**Improve.**
294	IC — every correction you make, push back into your story or prompt so you never make it twice. Lead — push corrections into the *shared* rules layer so the *squad* never makes them again. This is your highest-leverage move.
295	
296	**Protect quality.**
297	IC — your commit is clean (no `any`, no hex, three states). Lead — the bar holds across the codebase *under deadline pressure*, including when holding it is inconvenient.
298	
299	**Manage context.**
300	IC — one topic per thread; named threads; short threads. Lead — decide what's personal-thread vs shared-artifact and make it explicit, so team knowledge lives in the Project and rules layer, not in someone's chat history.
301	
302	**Handle uncertainty.**
303	IC — flag what you (or Claude) are unsure of rather than inventing; distinguish "verified" from "assumed." *(This is already how you work — it's your verification mindset. Keep it.)* Lead — make "flag, don't invent" a team norm; keep an open-items list visible; never let an assumption harden into a fact silently.
304	
305	**Multiply / mentor.**
306	IC — you get faster and cleaner. Lead — *the room* gets faster and cleaner because of how you work. You are the capability anchor; knowledge you don't transfer is a single point of failure wearing your name.
307	
308	**Think beyond.**
309	IC — the next component, the next state, the downstream effect of a data-shape choice. Lead — what happens when you're *not in the room*: the team you're growing, the second squad's dependencies, the integration seams, the go-live risk, the two-year maintainability of every convention you set.

363	## 14. Rituals to run — review culture as delivery practice
364	
365	The training's *regroup* is your review culture. On the project you're the facilitator, under real stakes. Run it deliberately:
366	
367	- **Every work block gets a regroup.** Build, then look at real work together. The regroup exists *to learn from the work, not to judge the person who wrote it* — say that out loud and mean it. This norm is the whole thing; without it people hide their work and you lose visibility.
368	- **Rotate who's on screen.** Don't only review the confident volunteers — deliberately surface work from people who haven't been seen. (The training literally cold-picks, and bribes volunteers with snacks. Do the humane version: make it safe, make it normal, make it everyone.)
369	- **Ask structural questions, not surface ones.** "Is this well-written?" is the wrong question. "What will Claude *do* with this?" is the right one. Push people from fixing words to fixing structure.
370	- **Rolling verbal reviews, not just projector sessions.** One person shares one surprising flag; the room reacts. Cheap, frequent, low-ceremony.
371	- **The showcase is honest, not polished.** When you demo up or across, show what was *built*, not what you were *trying* to build. The single most valuable thing to surface is *"one thing the AI got right that followed from our rules, and one thing we corrected and why"* — the correction is the more important half. Model this; it sets the honesty bar for the squad.
372	- **Commitments are specific enough to check.** "Use Claude more" is not a commitment. *"Write the AC before I open Claude Code, not after"* is. Hold yourself and the squad to actionable specificity — the kind someone could verify in three months.

420	
421	**Still accurate, now with real names attached:** the rules layer as a **shared, two-squad contract** (not personal memory) remains arguably your single highest-leverage responsibility as FE Lead — this is the scale gap from §0. That contract isn't just written down, either — it's mechanically enforced: root `CODEOWNERS` maps every tier to a real GitHub team (`@ZimmermannAU/tier-1-approvers`, `tier-2-approvers`, `pwa-squad-a`, `pwa-squad-b`), and branch protection blocks a merge without the right team's review. §2's "Decide → set the convention so nobody re-litigates it" has a literal, checkable answer on this project: whichever `CODEOWNERS` says — assuming it agrees with the rest of the rules layer, which §16.4 shows it doesn't always. The regroup culture (§14) is still your cross-squad review cadence, run on your sprint/PI rhythm. Descope-never-cut, the 20-min rule, and deploy-first still directly protect margin on a fixed-price engagement. And the CI-CD gates are real and confirmed: `qa.yml` (Vitest + Storybook a11y, every PR into `develop`/`release/**`) and `digital-sit.yml` — the composite "Digital SIT Gate" (Playwright P0 + bundle-size + Lighthouse CI) on `release/**`. NewStore's OMS SIT runs as a genuinely parallel, non-blocking lane that only converges with Digital at the Stage tier — the original "Digital SIT; NewStore SIT" framing was directionally right; now you have the actual workflow files to point to.
422	
423	### 16.2 Corrections — claims that didn't hold up
424	
425	- **"14 integrations, four connector patterns routing through MuleSoft" — wrong, drop it.** No document in the repo supports either number. The real count is **18 PWA-layer integrations** (`.docs/temp/integration/index.md`, confirmed by `.docs/memory/projectState.md`'s status table), or **~28** including server-to-server/out-of-band systems (`.docs/architecture.md`'s full integration map — Avalara, Transperfect, Zendesk, Feedonomics, and others). Even `.docs/temp/openItems.md` contradicts itself — its prose says "fifteen," its own table and total line say 18. Cite "18 PWA-layer integrations" and drop the connector-pattern count entirely; the real MuleSoft routing is heterogeneous per integration (GiveX alone uses three different MuleSoft-involving paths depending on validate/redeem/issue/balance).
426	- **The "shared AI brain" isn't real — don't cite it as infrastructure.** `.docs/planning/sharedAiBrainBrief.md` proposes a pgvector/RAG knowledge base with its own MCP server and a `/knowledge` skill. It was never built — no fifteenth skill, no vector DB, nothing. What *is* real and does the Confluence/Jira-connectivity job it was reaching for: a plain `mcp-atlassian` MCP server, configured in root `.mcp.json`, giving Claude Code direct Jira/Confluence read/write with none of the semantic-search ambition. Don't oversell the aspiration to the squad as if it shipped.
427	- **The account-level instructions baseline from §4 doesn't exist as a file yet.** There is no committed prose instructions document anywhere in `manndotfiles` or elsewhere on this machine — verified directly. What you actually have is *tool configuration*: `claude/settings.seed.json` sets a global `effortLevel: "high"` dial, and your curated plugin list (`superpowers`, `code-review`, `pr-review-toolkit`) pulls in skills that already push back on rubber-stamping by design (e.g. `superpowers:receiving-code-review` explicitly requires "technical rigor and verification, not performative agreement"). That's a real, working approximation — but if you want the actual instructions-file baseline §4 describes, closing that gap means writing it, not assuming it's already there.
428	
429	### 16.3 Real capabilities the original bridge never mentioned
430	
431	Things that exist in the repo today that neither the training nor the original bridge covered:
432	
433	- **The auto-generated registry** (`.claude/registry/`, §16.1) — check it before every build per §9.4, and trust it more than any hand-written doc, since it can't go stale.
434	- **Five automation hooks** (`.claude/hooks/`): `tier2Warn.sh`, `contentfulDriftWarn.sh`, `registryUpdate.sh`, `testFileRemind.sh`, and `session-reflect.sh` (the doc-proposal drafter from §16.1), wired into `.claude/settings.json` across PreToolUse/PostToolUse/Stop events. Together they already enforce pieces of your quality bar mechanically — check `.claude/settings.json` for exactly which hook fires on which event before assuming something still needs a manual check.
435	- **CodeRabbit** (`coderabbit.yaml`, Tier 1) — a second, independent AI reviewer wired into the PR flow, separate from anything Claude Code does. Your review culture (§14) has two AI reviewers plus human review in the loop, not one.
436	- **`weekly-agents.yml`** — despite the name, this runs no AI agent. It's a scheduled job that sweeps for components missing tests/stories, audits orphaned Contentful definitions, and reminds open release PRs to run `/generate-changelog`. Don't describe it to the squad as "an AI agent" — it's plain automation with a misleading filename.
437	- **The rules layer isn't Claude-Code-exclusive.** `scripts/syncCursorRules.mjs` mirrors `.claude/rules/` and `.claude/skills/` out to `.cursor/rules/skills/*.mdc` and `.vscode/instructions/workflows.md`. If anyone on either squad works in Cursor or plain VS Code instead of Claude Code, the same conventions still reach them — worth knowing if you're relying on the rules layer as your enforcement mechanism across the whole squad, not just Claude Code users.
438	
439	### 16.4 Your first gap-hunts — live, unresolved contradictions
440	
441	Section 7 says to find every gap before Claude Code does. Here are three already sitting in the repo, found by cross-referencing real sources against each other. None are resolved below — that's deliberate, and it's a call for you and the leads, not something to silently pick a side on in a document.
442	
443	**1. Who owns Home, PDP, and PLP?**
444	- `squadA.md`, `squadB.md`, and `.docs/memory/sprintScope.md` all say **Squad A**.
445	- Root `CODEOWNERS`, the auto-generated `.claude/registry/pages.md`, and three skills (`onboarding`, `feature-spec`, `qa-generate`) all say **Squad B**.
446	- Everyone agrees cart/checkout is Squad A and search/account is Squad B — the fault line is specifically Home/PDP/PLP.
447	
448	**2. May Claude write directly to memory and rules files, or must it always propose first?**
449	- `.claude/hooks/session-reflect.sh`, a Stop hook, says Claude must *never* edit `.docs/memory/*`, `.claude/rules/*`, or PRDs directly — only draft a dated proposal into `.docs/agents-proposals/` for a human to review and apply by hand.
450	- `.claude/skills/session-start`'s own instructions describe writing to memory files directly, the moment something worth recording comes up.
451	- `frozenFiles.md`'s Tier-1 governance list doesn't include `.docs/memory/*` at all — the file-protection tier that would normally justify the hook's "never direct-edit" stance.
452	- This one is sharper than #1 — it's not just about who reviews a PR, it's about what Claude is actually allowed to do unprompted on this repo, and the answer currently depends on which doc a session happens to read first.
453	
454	**3. Are the `.docs/prompts/` build-prompt templates actually "done"?**
455	- All three carry a `Status — done. Kept for traceability.` banner.
456	- Each one lists doc-artifact paths under a bare `docs/` directory as part of what it produced — and that directory doesn't exist anywhere in this repo. (The code/config artifacts they describe — `digital-sit.yml`, `playwright.config.js`, `.browserstack.yml`, and others — are all real and verified; only the documentation half of the "done" claim is stale, likely left behind by the project's later move to Confluence.)
457	- This is the literal version of §7's own question: *"Is that gap fixed now, or did you just acknowledge it?"* These files acknowledged a plan and marked themselves done. Nobody went back to check.
458	
459	All three are the "is this a rule Claude can check against, or an aspiration it will ignore" failure mode from §6 — except worse, because each would pass a casual read. #1 would route a PR to the wrong reviewer, or have `audit-tier` tell someone a file is safe to touch alone when it isn't. #2 means two Claude Code sessions on this same repo could legitimately behave differently depending on which rule they happened to read first. #3 means a document you'd otherwise trust as "done" is quietly missing half of what it claims. Acknowledging all three in this paragraph isn't the fix, per §7's own distinction — the fix is whichever file actually changes.
460	
461	### 16.5 The honest close
462	
463	The training gave you a *transferable methodology* and proved it on a solo React build. Your job takes that methodology into **shared-codebase, two-squad, fixed-price delivery on a stack you don't yet have deep muscle memory in.** The discipline carries over completely. The framework fluency and the leadership craft are the two things you have to build deliberately on top of it.
464	
465	What's different now versus when this section was first written: you're no longer bridging from a solution deck. The repo is real, most of what it needed has already been read once, end to end, and the gaps that remain (§16.2's corrections, §16.4's contradiction) are *knowable* — which, per §7, means they're closeable. This document is only useful if you actually close them, not just read that they exist.
466	
467	The quality ceiling is set by you. So set it high, and hold it when it's inconvenient.
468
