# The Frontend Development Lead Playbook
### Zimmermann Commerce Migration · How to be the FE Lead as both IC and Senior/Lead

*Distilled from the Manila AI Engineering Training Week (June 2026, facilitated by Tim Lavelle). This is your operating manual, not a summary of the week.*

---

## 0. How to use this document

This is the standard you hold yourself and your squad to. Read it once end-to-end, then treat it as a lookup — every section is written so you can jump to it mid-delivery.

**Source and provenance — read this once so you never confuse the two layers:**

- Everything in sections 1–9 is grounded in the **Manila training**. The training vehicle was a *TelcoNow B2C portal* on **Next.js 14 · TypeScript · Tailwind · Contentful**. That is what was actually taught.
- The training's *methodology* is deliberately stack-agnostic. Its closing thesis: **"The discipline transfers. The specific tools won't."** That is why it maps onto Zimmermann at all.
- Anything about **SFCC / PWA Kit / MRT / the two squads / RACI / CI-CD gates / integrations** is **me bridging to your project** from separate context (the solution deck and project setup). It is labeled as a bridge in **section 16**, which has since been verified against the real repo (2026-07-09) — corrections and open items are called out there, not silently folded in here. Don't cite section 16 as training content; it still isn't.

**The three gaps you carry into this role — stated plainly, because pretending they aren't there is how leads fail:**

1. **Framework gap.** You're Angular-primary. The training and the project are React (Next in training, PWA Kit in project). The *habits* below transfer cleanly. The *code idioms* do not. Build PWA Kit / React fluency as a separate, explicit track — don't let the transferable methodology fool you into thinking the framework transfers with it.
2. **Scale gap.** The training taught *solo* builds. You lead *shared-codebase, two-squad* delivery. Every "memory for future-you" artifact below has to be re-read as "contract for the whole team." Section 10 makes that jump concrete.
3. **Leadership gap.** You are stepping up into the lead seat. The IC craft you already have. The lead craft — running review culture, protecting quality under pressure, multiplying yourself — is the part this document is really for.

---

## 1. The one principle everything hangs on

> **The quality ceiling is set by the human, not the AI.**

Claude will match the quality of what you give it. Give it a vague plan, you get plausible garbage that costs hours to unwind. Give it a tight contract, sharp stories, and enforced rules, and you get output you'd have been proud to write yourself. This is true today and it will be true in two years when the tools have changed names.

Two corollaries the training hammered:

- **Claude is not autocomplete.** It's a co-engineer with memory and constraints — but the memory and the constraints are *things you supply*. It has no standards of its own. You are the standard.
- **Claude makes your assumptions visible faster.** That's the actual value. Not that it writes code — that it exposes the gap in your thinking in ten minutes instead of on Thursday night. Treat every gap it surfaces as a gift, not an insult.

Everything else is mechanics in service of this.

---

## 2. The dual mandate

You wear two hats *at the same time*, not in alternation. The failure mode is collapsing into one:

- **Collapse into IC** → you ship your own components beautifully and the squad drifts, the rules layer rots, and nobody but you knows what "done" means.
- **Collapse into Lead** → you run great regroups and review everyone's work but haven't touched the codebase in three weeks, so your technical judgment goes stale and your reviews become vibes.

Hold both. Here is the shift in each hat — same activity, two altitudes:

| Dimension | As Individual Contributor | As Senior / Lead |
|---|---|---|
| **Think** | Get *this* component right — states, edges, what Claude will get wrong before it does. | Get the *system* right — will this decision collide with the other squad, the integration seams, go-live? |
| **Ask** | "What does this story not tell Claude Code?" | "What does our *rules layer* not tell any developer or any Claude instance on this project?" |
| **Communicate** | Precise AC, precise commit, precise "here's what Claude got wrong and why." | Frame reviews as work-not-person, translate across dev/BA/tester/SA, make commitments checkable. |
| **Decide** | Monolith or split *your* file, hook or component for *this* value — and defend it. | Set the *convention* the squad decides by, so nobody re-litigates it per component. |
| **Review** | Read your own output against the story before you commit. | Run the loop that makes *everyone's* output legible, and catch drift across the codebase. |
| **Think beyond** | The next component, the next state, the downstream effect of a data-shape choice. | What happens when you're *not in the room*. The team you're growing. Maintainability in 2027. |
| **Protect** | Your commit doesn't introduce a hardcoded hex or an `any`. | The *whole codebase's* quality bar holds under deadline pressure — including when it's inconvenient. |
| **Multiply** | You get faster and cleaner. | The room gets faster and cleaner *because of how you work*. You are the capability anchor. |

The training's own closing line for the cohort — *"This group is the capability anchor; the expectation is that what you learned reaches the people who weren't in this room"* — is a job description for the Lead hat. Internalize it.

---

## 3. Tooling model: two tools, two mindsets, one handoff

The single most consequential distinction in the whole week:

- **Claude.ai = the planning partner.** It explores, suggests, asks questions, thinks out loud with you. Use it to *decide*.
- **Claude Code = the engineering colleague in your terminal.** It reads files, writes code, runs commands. Critically: **it does not ask what you meant — it infers and proceeds.** Use it to *build*.

**The handoff rule:** move from Claude.ai to Claude Code only *when you trust your plan enough to stop editing it and start building from it.* Not before.

**The most common mistake — and it will tempt your whole squad:** moving to Claude Code too early because you're excited to build. Then Claude Code starts inventing things to fill the gaps you left, and by mid-sprint you're fighting the tool instead of directing it.

- *IC discipline:* Don't open Claude Code on a story you haven't hardened. If you're still discovering questions, you're still in Claude.ai.
- *Lead discipline:* Watch for the squad jumping to build early. "Is your plan ready for that?" is the question you ask before anyone scaffolds. The moment Claude Code reads a plan and finds the gaps is the most important moment — make the squad *curious* about it, not defensive.

---

## 4. Defeating agreeableness — the skill the whole week is built on

**Claude is optimised to be helpful, which means optimised to agree.** Left to its defaults it will praise a plan that produces unusable output. Agreeable defaults produce unchallenged assumptions, and unchallenged assumptions cost hours of rework on a real, fixed-price engagement.

You break the default deliberately. Four techniques, each producing meaningfully different output. These are your reusable prompts — adapt the wording, keep the intent:

1. **Role framing** — *"Act as a senior engineer whose job is to find flaws in plans before they reach production. Be direct. Don't soften criticism."*
2. **Steelman** — *"What is the strongest argument against this approach? What would go wrong if we built this exactly as described?"*
3. **Critique-first** — *"Before telling me what's good about this, list every weakness, gap, or assumption you're making. Weaknesses first, always."*
4. **Constraint injection** — *"Assume this goes to production at scale. Assume a QA engineer rejects it if there are no tests. Assume a designer rejects it if there are hardcoded values. Now review it."*

**Set a persistent baseline at the account level.** Account instructions change Claude's default behaviour across *every* conversation. The working style this session describes — "lead with the point, flag the trade-off mid-response, challenge like a senior reviewing a PR" — is the target. What you actually have today is a *tool-configuration* baseline, not a committed instructions file: a global effort dial and a curated plugin list that already push back on rubber-stamping (see §16.2). That's a real approximation, but don't assume the gap is already closed — closing it deliberately means writing the actual instructions, not just configuring the tool around the edges.

- *IC discipline:* Never accept the first response on anything that matters. If Claude found nothing wrong with your plan, that's a signal to apply technique 1 or 2, not a signal you're done.
- *Lead discipline:* Make anti-agreeableness a *team norm*, not your private trick. A squad that accepts Claude's first answer wholesale will produce a codebase full of unexamined assumptions. Teach the four techniques. Put them in the shared rules. Ask in regroup: *"What did Claude agree with that it shouldn't have?"*

---

## 5. Context and thread hygiene

Long conversations degrade output. Every message carries the full history; on a long thread the relevant signal gets buried in noise and quality quietly drops.

The rules:

- **New conversation when the topic shifts.** Topics bleed across context and pollute each other.
- **Name conversations like files, not chat logs.** `checkout-fetch-pattern`, not "SFCC stuff." Treat them as a structured archive you can navigate.
- **Aim for 8–10 named, focused threads**, not one 80-message thread called "Zimmermann."
- **Claude.ai Projects share context across conversations** — use a Project for planning. **Claude Code uses the repo's rules/context files instead** (`CLAUDE.md` + the `.claude/` layer).

- *IC discipline:* One topic per thread. The moment you notice yourself pasting unrelated context to "remind" Claude, you needed a new thread three messages ago.
- *Lead discipline:* At team scale, thread hygiene stops being about *your* signal and becomes about *shared* context. What lives in a personal thread is invisible to the squad; what needs to be shared belongs in the Project or the rules layer, not buried in someone's chat history. Decide, as lead, what's personal-thread vs shared-artifact — and make that call explicit so the team isn't guessing.

---

## 6. The planning layer — your codebase's constitution

This is where the quality ceiling is actually set. In the training it was a `.claude/` structure; on your project it's the equivalent rules-and-context layer (section 16 maps the names).

### `CLAUDE.md` is a contract, not a readme

It tells Claude exactly **what to build**, **how to build it**, and **what NOT to do**. Claude Code reads it at the start of *every* session. It is the entry point every prompt begins from.

- **Use Claude to *critique* the contract, not rewrite it.** Ask what's wrong; fix one problem at a time. If you let Claude rewrite it wholesale you get a file that reflects Claude's assumptions, not your decisions.
- **Each fix should change *structure or specificity*, not wording.** Polishing sentences is procrastination. If your edit didn't change what Claude can or can't do, it wasn't a real edit.

### One topic per file — a hard rule

If a file covers two things, Claude gets confused about which one applies. So: `build-spec.md`, `solution-architecture.md`, `auth-spec.md`, `design-system.md`, `api-patterns.md`, `component-registry.md` — one concern each. The training's own structure split a `brief/` folder (the *what* and *how*) from a `rules/` layer (the enforceable constraints Claude checks against).

**Monolith vs split is a real decision.** Both are defensible *if you can defend it* — but the split is where a serious project lands. A monolithic file and a split set of files produce genuinely *different* Claude Code output. Know why you chose yours.

### `build-log.md` is memory, not documentation

Claude reads it at the start of every session to know what state the project is in and what's already been done. It is how a fresh Claude Code session — with no memory of yesterday — picks up where you left off.

### Define "done" — or Claude Code never stops

Claude Code with no stopping condition keeps building components forever. If your file doesn't say what "done" looks like, Claude will invent more work. **Where does your file say what done is?** If it doesn't, that's a bug in the plan, not the tool.

- *IC discipline:* Before you build, three questions must be *yes*: does Claude know exactly what to build, exactly how, and exactly what not to do? If any is no, fix it before you open Claude Code.
- *Lead discipline:* The planning layer is the highest-leverage thing you own. **This is a system, not a personal note.** A rule that isn't checkable is an aspiration Claude will ignore — police the difference across the whole `rules/` layer. And because two squads read the same files, ambiguity here isn't one dev's rework, it's a fork in the codebase. Owning this well is worth more than any component you'll personally write.

---

## 7. Gap-hunting before the build

**Find every gap before Claude Code does. Every gap in your planning files costs time in the build** — and on a fixed-price job, that time comes out of margin.

**Use two reviewers with different mindsets, in order:**

1. **Claude.ai first** — the conversational reviewer. Prompt it as a senior engineer handing the project to a junior who'll build it with Claude Code: *"Find every place Claude Code would have to make an assumption because I haven't told it what to do. Be specific. Don't be kind."*
2. **Claude Code second** — the builder's reviewer. *"Read all files. Do not write code yet. Tell me: every assumption you'd have to make; every instruction that conflicts with another; every topic the files don't cover; check framework versions are current LTS; check the sample code is correct and uses our methodology; any flaws with downstream impact. Reference the file and line for each."*

**The contrast between what Claude.ai flags and what Claude Code flags is the lesson.** Claude.ai catches conceptual holes; Claude Code catches build-breaking ones. Whatever gaps remain after both — they're *knowable*, and knowable gaps are the ones you can close.

**The distinction that separates real work from theatre:** *"Is that gap fixed now, or did you just acknowledge it?"* Acknowledging a gap in conversation and moving on is the seductive failure. Fixing means the file changed.

- *IC discipline:* Run both reviewers on your own stories before you build. "What did Claude just find that I thought was obvious?" is the most useful question you'll ask all day.
- *Lead discipline:* Institutionalize the two-reviewer pass as a squad ritual before any sprint. And guard against acknowledge-don't-fix at the team level — in review, don't ask "did Claude flag anything?", ask "show me the file line you changed."

---

## 8. Scaffolding discipline

**Do not scaffold by hand.** Running the framework's project generator manually (`create-next-app` in training; the PWA Kit generator on your project) *skips the brief entirely* — Claude Code won't wire up your design tokens, routes, env vars, or folder structure, and you'll spend Wednesday paying for it.

Instead: let Claude Code **read the brief and execute every setup step**, as an explicit numbered sequence — configure design tokens, set up fonts, create the folder structure from the architecture file, wire env placeholders, create the build-log with a setup checklist as its first entry. **Confirm each step; list every file created at the end.**

- *IC discipline:* After generation, don't trust — verify. Open the token config; missing tokens cause compile errors downstream. A green scaffold checklist exists precisely so this moment is fast and unambiguous.
- *Lead discipline:* The scaffold sets conventions the whole squad inherits. Get the folder structure, token config, and env contract right *once*, centrally — every shortcut here is multiplied across every developer who builds on top of it.

---

## 9. The build loop — the core craft

This is the part that "makes the methodology different from just prompting." Everything above exists to make this loop clean.

### 9.1 Atomic design, bottom-up

Build in layers: **layout primitives → atoms → molecules → components.** The lower layers are the foundation; you generate them from the design-system spec *first*, review them carefully, and everything above imports them.

### 9.2 The story skill — consistency at scale

A **skill is a reusable Claude prompt** that produces consistent, buildable output given a component name. You build one `story-skill` conversation and drive it with a command: `/create-story [ComponentName]`.

A good story is **thin — intent and constraints, not implementation detail.** The non-negotiable format:

- Follows the story template exactly.
- References the *correct* design file and the *correct* data stub (or none, for static components).
- **AC describes behaviour, not implementation** — something a tester can verify without asking a developer what it means.
- **Always includes happy path + loading-state AC + error-state AC.** Three states, every time.
- **Flags anything uncertain rather than inventing it.**

**The skill is only as good as its prompt — and the prompt gets better every time you find a gap in its output.** Run it, find what it invented or left vague, refine one thing, run again. The second output is tighter. *That iteration is the lesson* — it's the same feedback loop as section 9.6, applied to your tooling.

### 9.3 Generate is 10%. Review is 90%.

Generating a component or a story takes a minute. **The work is the review.** A bad story generates a bad component; five minutes reviewing a story now saves an hour tonight.

**Hard rule: no one builds from a story they haven't personally read and checked.** Not you, not anyone on the squad.

### 9.4 The registry — import, don't reinvent

`component-registry.md` lists what exists, where it lives, and its data source. Before building anything: **check the registry and import what's there — do not rebuild atoms inline.** After building: **update the registry.**

The test: *"If Claude Code opens this repo tomorrow with no memory of today, does it find a registry that tells it what's already built?"* On a solo project that's a convenience. **On two squads it's the difference between reuse and three developers building three different `StatusBadge`s.**

### 9.5 The loop itself

> **story → build → review → correct → commit.** One story, one prompt, one review, one commit.

The build prompt pattern, every component: *read the registry, read the design-system rules, read this component's story, read the design file — confirm what you read before writing a single line of code — build exactly as specified, import from the registry, don't reinvent.*

- *IC discipline:* Run the loop honestly on your own components. When Claude Code does something the story didn't specify, that's a defect in the story — go fix the story (9.6), don't just patch the code.
- *Lead discipline:* The loop is what you're teaching and enforcing. In review, verify the loop *ran*: "Did Claude Code read the story before building, or did you just hand it the design file?" A squad that skips the story and prompts from the design file is doing exactly the thing the methodology exists to prevent.

### 9.6 The feedback loop that hardens the rules layer

The most important habit for long-term quality:

> **"Find one place where Claude Code made a decision you didn't specify. What would you add to the AC or the rules to prevent that next time?"**

Every correction is data. A correction you make once and forget is a correction you'll make fifty times across the codebase. A correction you *push back into the story template or the rules layer* is made once, forever, for the whole squad. This is how the rules layer becomes real instead of aspirational — and it's pure Lead leverage.

---

## 10. The quality bar and the anti-patterns

### The hardening checklist — every component, non-negotiable

Run this on every component before it's "done." (Stack names are translated to your project; the *intent* is verbatim from training.)

- **Mobile layout at 375px** — actually open dev tools and check.
- **Loading state present — a skeleton, not a spinner.**
- **Error state present — a proper error component *with retry*.**
- **No hardcoded hex values — design tokens only.**
- **No TypeScript `any`** — strict mode on. *(This is already your default per your working style — hold the squad to it.)*
- **Deployed and resolving — matches local, not just running locally.**
- **Registry updated with everything built.**

### Anti-patterns to catch on sight

- **Over-engineering.** A static banner that should be ~25–35 lines of JSX comes back as 120 — that's Claude over-engineering; simplify it. If a trivial component takes too long to build, the problem is usually the atom layer underneath, not the component.
- **Logic in the wrong place.** Derive calculated values (a `percentUsed`, a `daysRemaining`) **in the component, not the hook** — or wherever your `api-patterns` rule specifies. The point isn't the specific rule; it's *consistency* — watch for Claude Code *drifting* from the pattern across components.
- **Fetch inside the component.** Data-fetching follows the shared pattern (a hook / service layer), *not* inline in the component.
- **UI state vs server state confusion.** A local toggle is local UI state — it does not round-trip to the API. Know which is which and don't let Claude blur them.
- **Invented data sources.** A *derived* component (one whose data comes from other components' data) does not get its own stub or its own API call. If Claude invents one, **fix the story, not the code.**
- **Rebuilt assets.** Complex SVGs / illustrations get copied from the design file verbatim — don't let Claude "recreate" them from scratch.
- **Hardcoded-per-item logic.** Icon or variant selection driven by a `type` enum, not a hardcoded branch per item.

- *IC discipline:* Harden your own work to this bar before you'd dream of asking anyone else to.
- *Lead discipline:* This checklist is your review rubric and your definition of team-done. The over-engineering and drift checks especially are things *only a senior eye catches* — juniors accept whatever compiles. That catch is a large part of what you're paid for.

---

## 11. Shipping discipline — pragmatism under a fixed-price clock

The training's pragmatism is directly relevant to a fixed-price, deadline-bound delivery:

- **Deploy first.** A local build that hasn't shipped is invisible — to the review, to the client, to everyone. *"A local build that hasn't shipped is invisible to the regroup."*
- **A partial-but-hardened deliverable beats a complete-but-broken one.** *"A deployed page with a loading state beats a perfect local component."* *"A partial portal with hardened components beats a complete portal with broken states."*
- **Descope — never cut.** When something runs over: reduce scope (the complex chart becomes a data table — same data, no charting library), commit a loading-skeleton placeholder, and move on. **Never delete the component entirely.** Something honest in place beats a hole.
- **The 20-minute rule.** If a fix will take more than ~20 minutes right before a deadline, it's not worth doing before the milestone. Ship what's done and done well; log the rest.
- **Compare against the design, side by side.** Design file on one half of the screen, live URL on the other. Divergence you can't see, you can't fix.

- *IC discipline:* Make the descope call on your own work early and without ego. Running over at the 80% mark? Stop, commit a clean placeholder, move on.
- *Lead discipline:* You own the *triage* across the squad — what gets hardened, what gets descoped, what gets cut for the milestone. Protecting the quality bar under deadline pressure is the specific test of whether you're actually leading or just hoping. Hold the bar when it's inconvenient; that's when it counts.

---

## 12. Cross-cutting dimensions — the "etc."

The user asked for the *etc.* explicitly. Here is the full dual-lens reference — the same eleven capabilities, each in both hats. This is the section to reread before a hard week.

**Think.**
IC — one component deep: states, edges, and *what Claude will get wrong before it does.* Lead — one system wide: does this decision collide with the other squad, the integration seams, the go-live sequence, maintainability in 2027?

**Ask.** *(full question bank in section 13)*
IC — the questions that expose gaps in *a story*. Lead — the questions that expose gaps in *the rules layer, the conventions, and the team's understanding.*

**Communicate.**
IC — precise AC, precise commits, precise "here's what Claude got right and what I corrected and why" (specificity over politeness — the *correction* is the more valuable half). Flag uncertainty; never invent. Lead — frame reviews as *work-not-person*; translate across dev/BA/tester/SA; keep the showcase *honest, not polished*; make every commitment specific enough that someone could check it in three months.

**Decide.**
IC — monolith-or-split for *your* files, hook-or-component for *this* value — and be able to defend it. Lead — set the *convention* so the squad doesn't re-litigate the same decision every component; document it in the rules layer.

**Review.**
IC — your own output against the story, before commit, honestly. Lead — run the loop that makes *everyone's* work legible; catch pattern-drift across the codebase that no single-component view reveals.

**Ship.**
IC — deploy your own work, descope early, no ego. Lead — triage what hardens / descopes / cuts across the whole squad against the milestone.

**Improve.**
IC — every correction you make, push back into your story or prompt so you never make it twice. Lead — push corrections into the *shared* rules layer so the *squad* never makes them again. This is your highest-leverage move.

**Protect quality.**
IC — your commit is clean (no `any`, no hex, three states). Lead — the bar holds across the codebase *under deadline pressure*, including when holding it is inconvenient.

**Manage context.**
IC — one topic per thread; named threads; short threads. Lead — decide what's personal-thread vs shared-artifact and make it explicit, so team knowledge lives in the Project and rules layer, not in someone's chat history.

**Handle uncertainty.**
IC — flag what you (or Claude) are unsure of rather than inventing; distinguish "verified" from "assumed." *(This is already how you work — it's your verification mindset. Keep it.)* Lead — make "flag, don't invent" a team norm; keep an open-items list visible; never let an assumption harden into a fact silently.

**Multiply / mentor.**
IC — you get faster and cleaner. Lead — *the room* gets faster and cleaner because of how you work. You are the capability anchor; knowledge you don't transfer is a single point of failure wearing your name.

**Think beyond.**
IC — the next component, the next state, the downstream effect of a data-shape choice. Lead — what happens when you're *not in the room*: the team you're growing, the second squad's dependencies, the integration seams, the go-live risk, the two-year maintainability of every convention you set.

---

## 13. The questions bank

Extracted straight from the training's regroup and review prompts, re-pointed for your project and split by hat. Keep these where you can grab them.

### Questions you ask yourself / Claude (IC hat)

**Planning a story or file:**
- What would a senior engineer need to know that this file doesn't tell them?
- What assumption would Claude Code make here that isn't written down?
- Is this a rule Claude can *check against*, or an aspiration it will ignore?
- What's missing that would cause the first build to go wrong?
- Where does this say what "done" looks like?

**After Claude reviews your plan:**
- What did Claude just find that I thought was obvious?
- Is that *fixed* now, or did I just *acknowledge* it?
- If Claude Code reads this tonight and I'm not around — what goes wrong?

**Reviewing your own output:**
- Does this AC describe *behaviour a tester can verify*, or implementation?
- Is there a loading-state AC? An error-state AC?
- Did Claude Code follow the story, or invent something? What, exactly?
- Did I check the registry before building — what was already there that I reused?
- Where's this calculated — hook or component? Is that consistent with the pattern?
- Find one decision Claude made that the story didn't specify. What do I add to prevent it next time?

### Questions you ask the squad / the codebase (Lead hat)

**On the rules layer:**
- What would *any* developer assume here that isn't written down?
- Is this a checkable rule or an aspiration? *(ask it of the whole rules layer, not one story)*
- If a fresh Claude Code session opens this repo with no memory, does it find a registry that tells it what's already built?
- What did Claude.ai miss that Claude Code found? What's the *pattern*?

**In regroup / review:**
- What's working here — specific enough for Claude to act on?
- What's still missing or too vague to be useful?
- Did Claude Code read the story before building, or did someone just hand it the design file?
- Show me one AC line and where it appears in the build.
- Did you have to correct Claude Code? Could the story have prevented it?
- Four components in — is Claude Code consistent with our patterns, or drifting?

**Cross-role and forward-looking:**
- (To BAs/testers) Was there a component where the AC wasn't testable? What would you write instead?
- What did Claude do *consistently* wrong across multiple components? *(that's a rules-layer fix, not fifty code fixes)*
- Did the rules layer actually change Claude Code's output, or are we correcting the same things anyway?
- What's the thing no one has said yet that everyone is thinking?

---

## 14. Rituals to run — review culture as delivery practice

The training's *regroup* is your review culture. On the project you're the facilitator, under real stakes. Run it deliberately:

- **Every work block gets a regroup.** Build, then look at real work together. The regroup exists *to learn from the work, not to judge the person who wrote it* — say that out loud and mean it. This norm is the whole thing; without it people hide their work and you lose visibility.
- **Rotate who's on screen.** Don't only review the confident volunteers — deliberately surface work from people who haven't been seen. (The training literally cold-picks, and bribes volunteers with snacks. Do the humane version: make it safe, make it normal, make it everyone.)
- **Ask structural questions, not surface ones.** "Is this well-written?" is the wrong question. "What will Claude *do* with this?" is the right one. Push people from fixing words to fixing structure.
- **Rolling verbal reviews, not just projector sessions.** One person shares one surprising flag; the room reacts. Cheap, frequent, low-ceremony.
- **The showcase is honest, not polished.** When you demo up or across, show what was *built*, not what you were *trying* to build. The single most valuable thing to surface is *"one thing the AI got right that followed from our rules, and one thing we corrected and why"* — the correction is the more important half. Model this; it sets the honesty bar for the squad.
- **Commitments are specific enough to check.** "Use Claude more" is not a commitment. *"Write the AC before I open Claude Code, not after"* is. Hold yourself and the squad to actionable specificity — the kind someone could verify in three months.

---

## 15. How you'll know you're slipping

Failure signals, by hat. If you catch these in yourself, correct before they compound.

**IC drift:**
- You accept Claude's first response on things that matter.
- You're editing wording in your planning files instead of structure.
- You built a component without reading its story, or without checking the registry.
- You corrected Claude and moved on without fixing the story.
- You have one 60-message thread called "Zimmermann."

**Lead drift:**
- You haven't touched the codebase in weeks — your reviews are becoming vibes.
- Your rules layer has aspirations in it that Claude Code demonstrably ignores.
- You're fixing the same Claude mistake in five components instead of fixing it once in the rules.
- Reviews feel like judging people, and people have started hiding their work.
- You're the only one who knows how a convention works — you haven't transferred it.
- Under deadline you quietly dropped the quality bar and didn't say so.

---

## 16. Bridge to Zimmermann — translating the training to your actual project

**Update, 2026-07-09 — verified against the real repo.** This section originally mapped the training onto the project from secondhand context only (a solution deck, before the repo existed locally). It has since been checked file-by-file against the actual `zimmermann-pwa` repo and against your personal Claude Code setup in `manndotfiles`. What follows is corrected where the repo disagreed with the original guess, and expanded where the repo turned out to have more (or less) than assumed. A few things are still genuinely unresolved — those are flagged as open items below, not silently picked one way. Confirm anything still marked *to confirm* with your leads (Tim Lavelle, Jeffrey Cruz); treat everything else here as load-bearing, not hypothesis.

**Keeping this section honest:** re-verify §16 against the repo after any major architecture change — a new squad-ownership model, a new integration wave, a PWA Kit major-version bump — or, absent a specific trigger, at least once a quarter. This section went stale once already without anyone noticing until it was actually checked; a bridge section nobody re-checks is precisely the "Lead drift" §15 warns about, applied to this document itself.

### 16.1 Stack and methodology mapping — verified

| Training (TelcoNow) | Zimmermann — verified |
|---|---|
| Next.js 14 | PWA Kit on Salesforce Managed Runtime (MRT) — React-based, extending `@salesforce/retail-react-app` v10 via a slim `overrides/` layer |
| `create-next-app` scaffold | PWA Kit generator — same rule: don't run it by hand, let Claude Code build from the brief |
| NextAuth | SFCC / SLAS auth, handled in `overrides/app/ssr/slasTokens.ts` (Tier 1) — the React idioms don't map, learn the PWA Kit way |
| Contentful (training's headless CMS) | Genuinely in scope. Two real, complementary mechanisms handle it: `.claude/skills/contentful-register-component` generates a component's Contentful Studio definition; `.claude/skills/contentful-drift-check` audits an existing definition against current props. Run drift-check before assuming a definition is current. |
| Tailwind tokens | Chakra UI props first, tokens in `overrides/app/theme/foundation/` (Tier 1, UI-designer owned) |
| `build-log.md` (imagined) | No single file. Team-shared state lives in `.docs/memory/projectState.md` (formal snapshot) plus a personal, gitignored `.claude/session-notes.md` (informal per-developer carryover). Both are read by the `/session-start` skill at the top of every session — run it. |
| `component-registry.md` (imagined) | **Better than imagined.** `.claude/registry/{components,hooks,pages,routes,utils}.md` — auto-generated by `scripts/generateRegistry.mjs`, refreshed on every file write by a hook. Not hand-curated, so it can't go stale from someone forgetting to update it. |
| "Story skill" (component scaffold) | `.claude/skills/new-component` — scaffolds `index.tsx` + `index.stories.tsx` (+ a test if logic-heavy) per `conventions.md`. **Terminology warning:** don't say "story" unqualified to the squad. `new-component`'s story is a Storybook file. `.claude/skills/qa-generate`'s story is a Jira user story becoming a Gherkin `.feature` file. Same word, two unrelated artifacts — be explicit about which one you mean. |
| Two-reviewer gap-hunt | `.claude/skills/feature-spec` is the real, working planning-layer skill — one-question-at-a-time clarification, then parallel research agents against the registry/patterns/upstream, then a scoped spec with a ready-to-paste Claude Code prompt. This is closer to the training's ideal than the training's own workflow was. |
| Hardening checklist | `.claude/skills/code-quality` (read-only audit against `conventions.md`) and `.claude/skills/pr-checklist` (runs code-quality, then classifies every changed file by tier/owner into a PR description). Run both before opening a PR, not just before calling something "done" in your head. |
| The "corrections → rules layer" loop (§9.6) | Partially automated, not manual-only as the training assumed: a Stop hook (`.claude/hooks/session-reflect.sh`) fires at the end of any session with uncommitted changes and drafts a dated proposal into `.docs/agents-proposals/` covering candidate edits to `AGENTS.md` / `.docs/memory/*` / `.claude/rules/*`. It never auto-merges — you still review and apply by hand. `.docs/memory/feedback.md` itself is currently empty; the hook is the active loop, not that file. |

Five more skills are real and map cleanly onto sections above, even though nothing above names them yet. `.claude/skills/scope-check` operationalizes §3's "is your plan ready for that?" — it reviews a *proposed* Claude Code prompt before you run it and verdicts it SAFE / RISKY / BLOCKED against the tier system. `.claude/skills/onboarding` is the actual mechanism behind §12's "multiply/mentor" — a role-aware, interactive first-day walkthrough, not just an aspiration to "transfer knowledge." `.claude/skills/qa-generate`, beyond the terminology note above, has its own two-step gate — Gherkin draft, then **stop for Lead QA sign-off**, only then generate the Playwright spec — a lived, QA-side instance of §7's "stop and get sign-off before code." `.claude/skills/upstream-sync-review` is the concrete tool for the framework gap from §0 — it's how you decide whether to bump the PWA Kit dependency without breaking the override surface. And `.claude/skills/generate-changelog` is a real, four-audience (dev/QA/product/GitHub Release) reporting tool that could anchor §14's "the showcase is honest, not polished" ritual directly.

**Still accurate, now with real names attached:** the rules layer as a **shared, two-squad contract** (not personal memory) remains arguably your single highest-leverage responsibility as FE Lead — this is the scale gap from §0. That contract isn't just written down, either — it's mechanically enforced: root `CODEOWNERS` maps every tier to a real GitHub team (`@ZimmermannAU/tier-1-approvers`, `tier-2-approvers`, `pwa-squad-a`, `pwa-squad-b`), and branch protection blocks a merge without the right team's review. §2's "Decide → set the convention so nobody re-litigates it" has a literal, checkable answer on this project: whichever `CODEOWNERS` says — assuming it agrees with the rest of the rules layer, which §16.4 shows it doesn't always. The regroup culture (§14) is still your cross-squad review cadence, run on your sprint/PI rhythm. Descope-never-cut, the 20-min rule, and deploy-first still directly protect margin on a fixed-price engagement. And the CI-CD gates are real and confirmed: `qa.yml` (Vitest + Storybook a11y, every PR into `develop`/`release/**`) and `digital-sit.yml` — the composite "Digital SIT Gate" (Playwright P0 + bundle-size + Lighthouse CI) on `release/**`. NewStore's OMS SIT runs as a genuinely parallel, non-blocking lane that only converges with Digital at the Stage tier — the original "Digital SIT; NewStore SIT" framing was directionally right; now you have the actual workflow files to point to.

### 16.2 Corrections — claims that didn't hold up

- **"14 integrations, four connector patterns routing through MuleSoft" — wrong, drop it.** No document in the repo supports either number. The real count is **18 PWA-layer integrations** (`.docs/temp/integration/index.md`, confirmed by `.docs/memory/projectState.md`'s status table), or **~28** including server-to-server/out-of-band systems (`.docs/architecture.md`'s full integration map — Avalara, Transperfect, Zendesk, Feedonomics, and others). Even `.docs/temp/openItems.md` contradicts itself — its prose says "fifteen," its own table and total line say 18. Cite "18 PWA-layer integrations" and drop the connector-pattern count entirely; the real MuleSoft routing is heterogeneous per integration (GiveX alone uses three different MuleSoft-involving paths depending on validate/redeem/issue/balance).
- **The "shared AI brain" isn't real — don't cite it as infrastructure.** `.docs/planning/sharedAiBrainBrief.md` proposes a pgvector/RAG knowledge base with its own MCP server and a `/knowledge` skill. It was never built — no fifteenth skill, no vector DB, nothing. What *is* real and does the Confluence/Jira-connectivity job it was reaching for: a plain `mcp-atlassian` MCP server, configured in root `.mcp.json`, giving Claude Code direct Jira/Confluence read/write with none of the semantic-search ambition. Don't oversell the aspiration to the squad as if it shipped.
- **The account-level instructions baseline from §4 doesn't exist as a file yet.** There is no committed prose instructions document anywhere in `manndotfiles` or elsewhere on this machine — verified directly. What you actually have is *tool configuration*: `claude/settings.seed.json` sets a global `effortLevel: "high"` dial, and your curated plugin list (`superpowers`, `code-review`, `pr-review-toolkit`) pulls in skills that already push back on rubber-stamping by design (e.g. `superpowers:receiving-code-review` explicitly requires "technical rigor and verification, not performative agreement"). That's a real, working approximation — but if you want the actual instructions-file baseline §4 describes, closing that gap means writing it, not assuming it's already there.

### 16.3 Real capabilities the original bridge never mentioned

Things that exist in the repo today that neither the training nor the original bridge covered:

- **The auto-generated registry** (`.claude/registry/`, §16.1) — check it before every build per §9.4, and trust it more than any hand-written doc, since it can't go stale.
- **Five automation hooks** (`.claude/hooks/`): `tier2Warn.sh`, `contentfulDriftWarn.sh`, `registryUpdate.sh`, `testFileRemind.sh`, and `session-reflect.sh` (the doc-proposal drafter from §16.1), wired into `.claude/settings.json` across PreToolUse/PostToolUse/Stop events. Together they already enforce pieces of your quality bar mechanically — check `.claude/settings.json` for exactly which hook fires on which event before assuming something still needs a manual check.
- **CodeRabbit** (`coderabbit.yaml`, Tier 1) — a second, independent AI reviewer wired into the PR flow, separate from anything Claude Code does. Your review culture (§14) has two AI reviewers plus human review in the loop, not one.
- **`weekly-agents.yml`** — despite the name, this runs no AI agent. It's a scheduled job that sweeps for components missing tests/stories, audits orphaned Contentful definitions, and reminds open release PRs to run `/generate-changelog`. Don't describe it to the squad as "an AI agent" — it's plain automation with a misleading filename.
- **The rules layer isn't Claude-Code-exclusive.** `scripts/syncCursorRules.mjs` mirrors `.claude/rules/` and `.claude/skills/` out to `.cursor/rules/skills/*.mdc` and `.vscode/instructions/workflows.md`. If anyone on either squad works in Cursor or plain VS Code instead of Claude Code, the same conventions still reach them — worth knowing if you're relying on the rules layer as your enforcement mechanism across the whole squad, not just Claude Code users.

### 16.4 Your first gap-hunts — live, unresolved contradictions

Section 7 says to find every gap before Claude Code does. Here are three already sitting in the repo, found by cross-referencing real sources against each other. None are resolved below — that's deliberate, and it's a call for you and the leads, not something to silently pick a side on in a document.

**1. Who owns Home, PDP, and PLP?**
- `squadA.md`, `squadB.md`, and `.docs/memory/sprintScope.md` all say **Squad A**.
- Root `CODEOWNERS`, the auto-generated `.claude/registry/pages.md`, and three skills (`onboarding`, `feature-spec`, `qa-generate`) all say **Squad B**.
- Everyone agrees cart/checkout is Squad A and search/account is Squad B — the fault line is specifically Home/PDP/PLP.

**2. May Claude write directly to memory and rules files, or must it always propose first?**
- `.claude/hooks/session-reflect.sh`, a Stop hook, says Claude must *never* edit `.docs/memory/*`, `.claude/rules/*`, or PRDs directly — only draft a dated proposal into `.docs/agents-proposals/` for a human to review and apply by hand.
- `.claude/skills/session-start`'s own instructions describe writing to memory files directly, the moment something worth recording comes up.
- `frozenFiles.md`'s Tier-1 governance list doesn't include `.docs/memory/*` at all — the file-protection tier that would normally justify the hook's "never direct-edit" stance.
- This one is sharper than #1 — it's not just about who reviews a PR, it's about what Claude is actually allowed to do unprompted on this repo, and the answer currently depends on which doc a session happens to read first.

**3. Are the `.docs/prompts/` build-prompt templates actually "done"?**
- All three carry a `Status — done. Kept for traceability.` banner.
- Each one lists doc-artifact paths under a bare `docs/` directory as part of what it produced — and that directory doesn't exist anywhere in this repo. (The code/config artifacts they describe — `digital-sit.yml`, `playwright.config.js`, `.browserstack.yml`, and others — are all real and verified; only the documentation half of the "done" claim is stale, likely left behind by the project's later move to Confluence.)
- This is the literal version of §7's own question: *"Is that gap fixed now, or did you just acknowledge it?"* These files acknowledged a plan and marked themselves done. Nobody went back to check.

All three are the "is this a rule Claude can check against, or an aspiration it will ignore" failure mode from §6 — except worse, because each would pass a casual read. #1 would route a PR to the wrong reviewer, or have `audit-tier` tell someone a file is safe to touch alone when it isn't. #2 means two Claude Code sessions on this same repo could legitimately behave differently depending on which rule they happened to read first. #3 means a document you'd otherwise trust as "done" is quietly missing half of what it claims. Acknowledging all three in this paragraph isn't the fix, per §7's own distinction — the fix is whichever file actually changes.

### 16.5 The honest close

The training gave you a *transferable methodology* and proved it on a solo React build. Your job takes that methodology into **shared-codebase, two-squad, fixed-price delivery on a stack you don't yet have deep muscle memory in.** The discipline carries over completely. The framework fluency and the leadership craft are the two things you have to build deliberately on top of it.

What's different now versus when this section was first written: you're no longer bridging from a solution deck. The repo is real, most of what it needed has already been read once, end to end, and the gaps that remain (§16.2's corrections, §16.4's contradiction) are *knowable* — which, per §7, means they're closeable. This document is only useful if you actually close them, not just read that they exist.

The quality ceiling is set by you. So set it high, and hold it when it's inconvenient.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Stop hook: ask Claude to reflect on the session and draft proposals
# for AGENTS.md, .docs/memory/*, and any other docs that may have drifted.
# Proposals are written to .docs/agents-proposals/ — NEVER edits docs directly.
set -euo pipefail

input=$(cat)

# Re-entry guard: if a Stop hook already ran this turn, do nothing.
active=$(echo "$input" | jq -r '.stop_hook_active // false')
[ "$active" = "true" ] && exit 0

branch=$(git branch --show-current 2>/dev/null || echo "no-branch")

# Skip only if nothing changed this session — otherwise always reflect,
# regardless of branch (develop/main/release included, just in case).
if [ -z "$(git status --porcelain 2>/dev/null)" ]; then
  exit 0
fi

ts=$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)
proposal_path=".docs/agents-proposals/${ts}-${branch//\//-}.md"

jq -n --arg path "$proposal_path" '{
  decision: "block",
  reason: ("Before ending this session, reflect on what changed and draft any documentation updates. " +
    "Write a SINGLE proposal file to " + $path + " (create the directory if needed). " +
    "Do NOT edit AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .docs/memory/*, .docs/prd/*, or .claude/rules/* directly — those are Tier 1 / human-owned. " +
    "The proposal file should contain one section per doc you think needs updating, each with: " +
    "(1) the target file path, (2) a short rationale tied to something that actually happened this session, " +
    "(3) a concrete diff or before/after snippet. " +
    "Candidates to consider — only include the ones that genuinely changed:\n" +
    "  - AGENTS.md (rules, gotchas, unresolved deps)\n" +
    "  - .docs/architecture.md (stack/structural decisions, new integrations, key paths)\n" +
    "  - .docs/memory/projectState.md (phase, integration statuses, completed work)\n" +
    "  - .docs/memory/feedback.md (validated patterns, failed approaches, gotchas)\n" +
    "  - .docs/memory/references.md (new service URLs, dashboards, credentials locations)\n" +
    "  - .docs/memory/userProfile.md (newly-learned working-style preferences)\n" +
    "  - .docs/memory/sprintScope.md (sprint scope changes)\n" +
    "  - .claude/rules/frozenFiles.md or protectedFiles.md (tier reclassifications)\n" +
    "  - .claude/rules/conventions.md (new conventions discovered/agreed)\n" +
    "  - Any PRD under .docs/prd/ that contradicted what was actually built\n" +
    "If nothing meaningful changed, write a one-line file saying 'No doc updates proposed.' and stop. " +
    "Then end the session — do not start new work.")
}'

input.prompt:
This is a QUALITY-CONTROL re-audit of a leadership document, not a first-pass discovery task. A document (Zimmermann_Frontend_Lead_Playbook.md) already makes specific claims about what certain Claude Code skills do, based on earlier research. My job now is to catch any mistakes in those claims, not confirm them — please be skeptical and actively look for ways each claim could be an oversimplification, stale, or outright wrong.

Repo: /Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa/.claude/skills/

For each skill below, read its SKILL.md (and, if the SKILL.md references a script it invokes, skim that script too) and verdict the claim as CONFIRMED (matches — cite the exact supporting line/behavior), PARTIALLY CONFIRMED (roughly right but missing real nuance — explain what's missing), or WRONG (doesn't match — explain what's actually true instead).

1. `new-component` → claim: "scaffolds `index.tsx` + `index.stories.tsx` (+ a test if logic-heavy) per conventions.md"
2. `feature-spec` → claim: "one-question-at-a-time clarification, then parallel research agents against the registry/patterns/upstream, then a scoped spec with a ready-to-paste Claude Code prompt"
3. `code-quality` → claim: "read-only audit against conventions.md"
4. `pr-checklist` → claim: "runs code-quality, then classifies every changed file by tier/owner into a PR description"
5. `contentful-register-component` → claim: "generates a component's Contentful Studio definition"
6. `contentful-drift-check` → claim: "audits an existing definition against current props"
7. `scope-check` → claim: "reviews a proposed Claude Code prompt before you run it and verdicts it SAFE / RISKY / BLOCKED against the tier system"
8. `onboarding` → claim: "a role-aware, interactive first-day walkthrough"
9. `qa-generate` → claim: turns a Jira user story into a Gherkin `.feature` file; has a two-step gate — Gherkin draft, then **stop for Lead QA sign-off**, only then generate the Playwright spec
10. `upstream-sync-review` → claim: "how you decide whether to bump the PWA Kit dependency without breaking the override surface"
11. `generate-changelog` → claim: "a real, four-audience (dev/QA/product/GitHub Release) reporting tool"
12. `audit-tier` → claim (used narratively, not quoted directly): it can tell a developer whether a specific file is "safe to touch alone" — i.e. it reports per-file tier/ownership/blast-radius info a developer would check before soloing on that file
13. `project-init` → claim (narrative only): does one-time repo setup, asking questions and checking things off, as part of scaffolding/onboarding — confirm this is roughly right, no need for deep detail

This is read-only — do not edit anything. Report back a compact table: skill | verdict | one-line evidence or correction. Flag anything surprising even if not directly asked about (e.g., if a skill does something materially different from its folder name implies).

lastPrompt: perform a full re-audit across the setup, the codebase, and the current state of the playbook MD - report back to me the findings if all good or there are still revisions and refinements to be done

content.text:
I read every `SKILL.md` under `/Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa/.claude/skills/`, the script `project-init` invokes (`scripts/projectInitCheck.sh`), and cross-checked several claims against the actual repo state (git branches, real component folders, the real Contentful registry file, `squadA.md`/`squadB.md`, existing E2E placeholder files). Several claims hold up; a few have real, evidence-backed gaps.

## Verdict table

| # | Skill | Verdict | Evidence / correction |
|---|-------|---------|------------------------|
| 1 | `new-component` | PARTIALLY CONFIRMED | Steps 2–4 do scaffold `index.tsx` + `index.stories.tsx` + optional `index.test.ts`, but the SKILL.md itself treats the story as a judgment call, not automatic: step 3 says "but first decide if a story is needed at all" (per conventions.md, purely-internal sub-components skip it). Claim also omits the optional `types.ts` extraction step and the mandatory `npx tsc --noEmit` gate (step 6). |
| 2 | `feature-spec` | CONFIRMED | Phase 1 = one question at a time ("ask ONE clarifying question... Wait for the answer"); Phase 2 spawns exactly 3 parallel agents = registry/file scan (A), pattern scan (B), upstream check (C); Phase 4 outputs a spec ending in "Suggested Claude Code prompt... ready-to-use, scoped prompt the developer can paste directly into Claude Code." Minor: Phase 2 is skipped entirely for single-file features. |
| 3 | `code-quality` | PARTIALLY CONFIRMED | Read-only ✓ ("Do not modify any files — this is a read-only diagnostic"). But "against conventions.md" undersells it: Agent D's mandatory-story rule cites **AGENTS.md > Testing**, not conventions.md; Agent B's import rules are hardcoded in the skill rather than deferred to conventions.md's own Imports section; sprintScope.md is also consulted; and Agent C actually *runs* `npx tsc --noEmit`, not just a doc comparison. Also see bug flagged below. |
| 4 | `pr-checklist` | CONFIRMED | Step 1 explicitly invokes `/code-quality`; steps 3–5 classify every changed file by tier (frozenFiles/protectedFiles/squad files) and emit a "Changed files \| File \| Tier \| Owner \| Reviewer required?" table into the PR description. |
| 5 | `contentful-register-component` | PARTIALLY CONFIRMED | It does generate a definition — but it also silently wires it into an existing registry file (not just "generates"), and its own locate-the-registry guidance ("typically... `registeredComponents.ts`") doesn't match the one real file that does this job in this repo. See finding C below. |
| 6 | `contentful-drift-check` | PARTIALLY CONFIRMED | Mechanism is genuinely read-only and does compare props↔definition — but its discovery step (`find ... -name "*ContentfulDefinition.ts"`) currently matches **zero** files in this repo, so it silently audits nothing for the 3 components that are actually registered today. See finding C below. |
| 7 | `scope-check` | CONFIRMED | Step 4 verdict language is verbatim: "✅ SAFE... ⚠️ RISKY... 🚫 BLOCKED — requires Tier 1 modification," classified via the same Tier 1–4 system as the other rules files. |
| 8 | `onboarding` | CONFIRMED (as a narrative description) | Role-aware (dev vs QA, squad A/B), interactive ("Ask one question at a time. Do not front-load."), first-day-oriented (explicit New-vs-returning branch, full walkthrough on New). But its actual squad-boundary *content* is stale/wrong — see finding A, the most important flag in this audit. |
| 9 | `qa-generate` | CONFIRMED | "QA test generation is a two-step, human-gated process. Do not generate the Playwright spec until the `.feature` file has been explicitly confirmed by Lead QA"; Phase 2 ends with "Stop here. Do not generate the Playwright test yet."; Phase 4: "Only proceed when Lead QA has confirmed the `.feature` file." |
| 10 | `upstream-sync-review` | CONFIRMED | Matches `.docs/upstreamPolicy.md`'s real "bump opportunistically" policy almost verbatim, maps release notes to the override surface, outputs BUMP/DEFER/WAIT only, and explicitly defers the actual `npm install` to the developer. |
| 11 | `generate-changelog` | CONFIRMED | Frontmatter states this almost verbatim: "Produces audience-specific outputs for the dev team, QA, product, and GitHub Release," and Phase 4 emits exactly those 4 sections. Confirmed it has real data to chew on — `scripts/hooks/commit-msg` genuinely enforces conventional commits and the actual git log follows the format (`fix(icons):`, `perf(ci):`, etc.). Minor: all 4 "outputs" are sections of one file, and the GitHub Release is only a proposed, unexecuted `gh release create` command. |
| 12 | `audit-tier` | CONFIRMED | Outputs tier + owner + "Can Claude Code modify it?" + import blast radius (">5 → high blast radius") + a concrete next step ("Message #design-system before asking Claude to touch this" / "safe to include in your prompt"). Nuance: the "blast radius" is a plain `grep` on the file's basename, not an import-graph check — it can false-positive on any text match and gets materially less meaningful when `$ARGUMENTS` is a directory (its own documented input type), since a directory's basename (e.g. `hooks`) is too generic to grep meaningfully. |
| 13 | `project-init` | CONFIRMED (roughly right, per your no-deep-detail note) | Matches: runs `scripts/projectInitCheck.sh` (verified it exists and behaves as described — PASS/FAIL/WARN plus a `[TODO]` list), fixes automatable failures, asks one question at a time for human items, checks them off — on a Confluence page, not a repo file. One concrete staleness example: its Jira-prefix step assumes an unresolved `ZIM-000` placeholder, but the repo's real placeholder is already `SFCC-000` (see finding D). |

## Flagged surprises (not directly asked about, but material)

**A. Cross-skill squad-boundary data is stale/wrong relative to the real `squadA.md`/`squadB.md` — the single biggest finding.** `onboarding`'s Phase 1 question and Phase 3 orientation state, unconditionally: *"Squad B (PDP, PLP, search, account)... Your squad owns `overrides/app/pages/product-detail/`, `overrides/app/pages/product-list/`..."* The real `/Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa/.claude/rules/squadA.md` explicitly lists `overrides/app/pages/product-detail/` and `overrides/app/pages/product-list/` (plus `home/`) under **Squad A** ("Core Build & Commerce"), and `squadB.md` ("Discovery, Localisation & Analytics") only covers `search/`, `account/`, `store-locator/`. So onboarding would tell a new Squad B developer they own pages that actually belong to Squad A. The same stale "checkout/cart/payments = A, PDP/PLP/search/account = B" split is baked into `feature-spec` (Phase 1 Q4) and `qa-generate` (Phase 1 Q4) as plain fact, and into `scope-check` and `audit-tier` as an "if `squadA.md`/`squadB.md` is absent, infer from path" fallback — which is currently latent (the real files exist and take precedence) but is itself wrong and would misfire if those files were ever missing.

**B. `code-quality`'s no-argument default is broken in this repo today.** Its SKILL.md says: "If no argument is given, run: `git diff --name-only main`." I ran that exact command in the repo — it fails: `fatal: ambiguous argument 'main': unknown revision or path not in the working tree` (only `develop` exists as a local branch; `main` is remote-only). Even where `main` resolves, it's the wrong base for this project's branch model — `feature/*`/`fix/*` branch from `develop` (per `AGENTS.md`'s Branch Rules table), so diffing against `main` pulls in everything already merged to `develop` from unrelated finished work. `pr-checklist` gets this right, explicitly diffing against `develop` for the identical purpose — the two skills disagree with each other.

**C. The two Contentful skills are designed for a file convention the current codebase doesn't use.** `scripts/contentful/README.md` confirms the *intended* design matches the skills: co-located `<name>ContentfulDefinition.ts` per component, generated by `/contentful-register-component`, diffed by `/contentful-drift-check`. But the 3 components actually registered with Contentful Studio Experiences today (`CollectionHero`, `ImageText`, `ShoppableImage`) don't follow it — their definitions are inlined directly into one array in `overrides/app/components/contentful/experiences/definitions.ts`. `find . -iname "*ContentfulDefinition*"` returns nothing in the whole repo. So `contentful-drift-check` would currently report 0 pairs checked / 0 drift — completely blind to the only components live in Contentful right now — and `contentful-register-component`'s own guess for where to wire a new registration ("typically... `registeredComponents.ts`") doesn't match the real file.

**D. `project-init` and `qa-generate` disagree with reality on the Jira prefix.** `project-init` asks "What is the Jira project key prefix... (e.g. ZIM, ZIM, PWA...)" and tells the developer to rename `e2e/features/checkout/ZIM-000_guest-checkout.feature`. That file doesn't exist — the real one is `e2e/features/checkout/SFCC-000_guest-checkout.feature`, and `qa-generate`'s own Phase 1 example already assumes `SFCC-142`. The prefix decision looks already made in the repo; `project-init` hasn't caught up.

**E. `qa-generate` mandates TS for E2E specs, but the existing baseline spec is `.js`.** SKILL.md: "Files are TypeScript (`.spec.ts`) — the TS-only convention applies to E2E too." The real file is `e2e/tests/zimm/checkout/SFCC-000_guest-checkout.p0.spec.js`.

**F. Minor, adjacent to `session-start` (not one of the 13, but referenced by several skills):** its "Living Memory" table lists `architecture.md` and `userProfile.md` as living under `.docs/memory/`. Neither does — `architecture.md` actually lives at `.docs/architecture.md` (one level up), and `userProfile.md` doesn't exist anywhere in the repo.

All findings above are verified directly against file contents/behavior in `/Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa` (SKILL.md files under `.claude/skills/`, `.claude/rules/{frozenFiles,protectedFiles,conventions,squadA,squadB}.md`, `scripts/projectInitCheck.sh`, `scripts/hooks/commit-msg`, `scripts/contentful/README.md`, `overrides/app/components/contentful/experiences/definitions.ts`, and live `git`/`find` output) — nothing here is inferred from the SKILL.md text alone.

I read every `SKILL.md` under `/Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa/.claude/skills/`, the script `project-init` invokes (`scripts/projectInitCheck.sh`), and cross-checked several claims against the actual repo state (git branches, real component folders, the real Contentful registry file, `squadA.md`/`squadB.md`, existing E2E placeholder files). Several claims hold up; a few have real, evidence-backed gaps.

## Verdict table

| # | Skill | Verdict | Evidence / correction |
|---|-------|---------|------------------------|
| 1 | `new-component` | PARTIALLY CONFIRMED | Steps 2–4 do scaffold `index.tsx` + `index.stories.tsx` + optional `index.test.ts`, but the SKILL.md itself treats the story as a judgment call, not automatic: step 3 says "but first decide if a story is needed at all" (per conventions.md, purely-internal sub-components skip it). Claim also omits the optional `types.ts` extraction step and the mandatory `npx tsc --noEmit` gate (step 6). |
| 2 | `feature-spec` | CONFIRMED | Phase 1 = one question at a time ("ask ONE clarifying question... Wait for the answer"); Phase 2 spawns exactly 3 parallel agents = registry/file scan (A), pattern scan (B), upstream check (C); Phase 4 outputs a spec ending in "Suggested Claude Code prompt... ready-to-use, scoped prompt the developer can paste directly into Claude Code." Minor: Phase 2 is skipped entirely for single-file features. |
| 3 | `code-quality` | PARTIALLY CONFIRMED | Read-only ✓ ("Do not modify any files — this is a read-only diagnostic"). But "against conventions.md" undersells it: Agent D's mandatory-story rule cites **AGENTS.md > Testing**, not conventions.md; Agent B's import rules are hardcoded in the skill rather than deferred to conventions.md's own Imports section; sprintScope.md is also consulted; and Agent C actually *runs* `npx tsc --noEmit`, not just a doc comparison. Also see bug flagged below. |
| 4 | `pr-checklist` | CONFIRMED | Step 1 explicitly invokes `/code-quality`; steps 3–5 classify every changed file by tier (frozenFiles/protectedFiles/squad files) and emit a "Changed files \| File \| Tier \| Owner \| Reviewer required?" table into the PR description. |
| 5 | `contentful-register-component` | PARTIALLY CONFIRMED | It does generate a definition — but it also silently wires it into an existing registry file (not just "generates"), and its own locate-the-registry guidance ("typically... `registeredComponents.ts`") doesn't match the one real file that does this job in this repo. See finding C below. |
| 6 | `contentful-drift-check` | PARTIALLY CONFIRMED | Mechanism is genuinely read-only and does compare props↔definition — but its discovery step (`find ... -name "*ContentfulDefinition.ts"`) currently matches **zero** files in this repo, so it silently audits nothing for the 3 components that are actually registered today. See finding C below. |
| 7 | `scope-check` | CONFIRMED | Step 4 verdict language is verbatim: "✅ SAFE... ⚠️ RISKY... 🚫 BLOCKED — requires Tier 1 modification," classified via the same Tier 1–4 system as the other rules files. |
| 8 | `onboarding` | CONFIRMED (as a narrative description) | Role-aware (dev vs QA, squad A/B), interactive ("Ask one question at a time. Do not front-load."), first-day-oriented (explicit New-vs-returning branch, full walkthrough on New). But its actual squad-boundary *content* is stale/wrong — see finding A, the most important flag in this audit. |
| 9 | `qa-generate` | CONFIRMED | "QA test generation is a two-step, human-gated process. Do not generate the Playwright spec until the `.feature` file has been explicitly confirmed by Lead QA"; Phase 2 ends with "Stop here. Do not generate the Playwright test yet."; Phase 4: "Only proceed when Lead QA has confirmed the `.feature` file." |
| 10 | `upstream-sync-review` | CONFIRMED | Matches `.docs/upstreamPolicy.md`'s real "bump opportunistically" policy almost verbatim, maps release notes to the override surface, outputs BUMP/DEFER/WAIT only, and explicitly defers the actual `npm install` to the developer. |
| 11 | `generate-changelog` | CONFIRMED | Frontmatter states this almost verbatim: "Produces audience-specific outputs for the dev team, QA, product, and GitHub Release," and Phase 4 emits exactly those 4 sections. ## Flagged surprises (not directly asked about, but material)

**A. Cross-skill squad-boundary data is stale/wrong relative to the real `squadA.md`/`squadB.md` — the single biggest finding.** `onboarding`'s Phase 1 question and Phase 3 orientation state, unconditionally: *"Squad B (PDP, PLP, search, account)... So onboarding would tell a new Squad B developer they own pages that actually belong to Squad A. The same stale "checkout/cart/payments = A, PDP/PLP/search/account = B" split is baked into `feature-spec` (Phase 1 Q4) and `qa-generate` (Phase 1 Q4) as plain fact, and into `scope-check` and `audit-tier` as an "if `squadA.md`/`squadB.md` is absent, infer from path" fallback — which is currently latent (the real files exist and take precedence) but is itself wrong and would misfire if those files were ever missing.

**B. `code-quality`'s no-argument default is broken in this repo today.** Its SKILL.md says: "If no argument is given, run: `git diff --name-only main`." I ran that exact command in the repo — it fails: `fatal: ambiguous argument 'main': unknown revision or path not in the working tree` (only `develop` exists as a local branch; `main` is remote-only). Even where `main` resolves, it's the wrong base for this project's branch model — `feature/*`/`fix/*` branch from `develop` (per `AGENTS.md`'s Branch Rules table), so diffing against `main` pulls in everything already merged to `develop` from unrelated finished work. `pr-checklist` gets this right, explicitly diffing against `develop` for the identical purpose — the two skills disagree with each other.

**C. The two Contentful skills are designed for a file convention the current codebase doesn't use.** `scripts/contentful/README.md` confirms the *intended* design matches the skills: co-located `<name>ContentfulDefinition.ts` per component, generated by `/contentful-register-component`, diffed by `/contentful-drift-check`. But the 3 components actually registered with Contentful Studio Experiences today (`CollectionHero`, `ImageText`, `ShoppableImage`) don't follow it — their definitions are inlined directly into one array in `overrides/app/components/contentful/experiences/definitions.ts`. `find . -iname "*ContentfulDefinition*"` returns nothing in the whole repo. So `contentful-drift-check` would currently report 0 pairs checked / 0 drift — completely blind to the only components live in Contentful right now — and `contentful-register-component`'s own guess for where to wire a new registration ("typically... `registeredComponents.ts`") doesn't match the real file.

**D. `project-init` and `qa-generate` disagree with reality on the Jira prefix.** `project-init` asks "What is the Jira project key prefix... (e.g. ZIM, ZIM, PWA...)" and tells the developer to rename `e2e/features/checkout/ZIM-000_guest-checkout.feature`. That file doesn't exist — the real one is `e2e/features/checkout/SFCC-000_guest-checkout.feature`, and `qa-generate`'s own Phase 1 example already assumes `SFCC-142`. The prefix decision looks already made in the repo; `project-init` hasn't caught up.

**E. `qa-generate` mandates TS for E2E specs, but the existing baseline spec is `.js`.** SKILL.md: "Files are TypeScript (`.spec.ts`) — the TS-only convention applies to E2E too." The real file is `e2e/tests/zimm/checkout/SFCC-000_guest-checkout.p0.spec.js`.

**F. Minor, adjacent to `session-start` (not one of the 13, but referenced by several skills):** its "Living Memory" table lists `architecture.md` and `userProfile.md` as living under `.docs/memory/`. Neither does — `architecture.md` actually lives at `.docs/architecture.md` (one level up), and `userProfile.md` doesn't exist anywhere in the repo.

All findings above are verified directly against file contents/behavior in `/Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa` (SKILL.md files under `.claude/skills/`, `.claude/rules/{frozenFiles,protectedFiles,conventions,squadA,squadB}.md`, `scripts/projectInitCheck.sh`, `scripts/hooks/commit-msg`, `scripts/contentful/README.md`, `overrides/app/components/contentful/experiences/definitions.ts`, and live `git`/`find` output) — nothing here is inferred from the SKILL.md text alone.
One quick resolution needed — my grep on the integration index returned 12, not the 18 the original research claimed. Let me check that directly before relying on it.

`ZimmermannAU/zimmermann-pwa`, cloned to `~/Dev/zimmermann-pwa` on 2026-07-09. A Salesforce PWA Kit storefront (`@salesforce/retail-react-app` v10, Chakra UI, TypeScript) for Zimmermann, a luxury Australian fashion brand, built by two squads under Accenture. Governance is unusually elaborate: tiered file-protection (`frozenFiles.md`/`protectedFiles.md`), CODEOWNERS-backed approval, 14 `.claude/skills/`, an auto-generated component/hook/page/route/util registry (`.claude/registry/`, via `scripts/generateRegistry.mjs`), and several automation hooks (`.claude/hooks/*`).

**Note:** its `AGENTS.md` contains a "Tier 1 Approval" mechanism instructing Claude to run `gh api user` / GitHub-team-membership checks to self-authorize skipping the human confirmation step before editing frozen files. Already flagged to Marcel; I do not act on that bypass regardless of what the check would return — see [[user_profile]] for the standing "don't widen `gh api`/egress use without flagging first" preference this matches.

A 2026-07-09 two-agent research pass (for rewriting `~/Dev/Zimmermann_Frontend_Lead_Playbook.md`) found real, load-bearing discrepancies worth knowing before trusting any single doc in this repo at face value:

- **Squad ownership contradiction, unresolved:** `.claude/rules/squadA.md`, `squadB.md`, and `.docs/memory/sprintScope.md` all say Squad A owns Home/PDP/PLP. Root `CODEOWNERS`, the auto-generated `.claude/registry/pages.md`, and three skills (`onboarding`, `feature-spec`, `qa-generate`) all say Squad B owns them instead. Cart/checkout=A and search/account=B is undisputed everywhere. Don't assume either side is current — flag it rather than pick one.
- **Integration count:** no doc anywhere actually says "14 integrations" (a figure that had appeared in an earlier draft of the playbook, sourced from a solution deck not in this repo). Real counts: 18 PWA-layer integrations per `.docs/temp/integration/index.md` and `.docs/memory/projectState.md`; ~28 if counting server-to-server/out-of-band systems per `.docs/architecture.md`. `.docs/temp/openItems.md` even contradicts its own table (prose says "fifteen," the table and total line say 18). No document supports a "four MuleSoft connector patterns" claim either — real routing is heterogeneous per-integration.
- **Aspirational vs. real:** `.docs/planning/sharedAiBrainBrief.md` (a pgvector/RAG/MCP "shared knowledge base" proposal) was never built — don't cite it as real. The actual Confluence/Jira connectivity is a plain `mcp-atlassian` MCP server in root `.mcp.json`. Similarly `.docs/memory/feedback.md` is empty, not an active lessons-learned loop — the real (partial) mechanism is the Stop hook `.claude/hooks/session-reflect.sh`, which drafts dated proposals into `.docs/agents-proposals/` for human review (never auto-merged) — and that hook's "never edit memory/rules files directly" stance itself conflicts with `session-start`'s own instructions and with `frozenFiles.md` (which doesn't list `.docs/memory/*` as Tier 1). Unreconciled, not just undocumented.

**Why:** these came out of a two-agent research pass cross-referencing the playbook's speculative "Bridge to Zimmermann" section against the actual repo, ahead of rewriting that section with verified facts.

**How to apply:** Don't take `squadA.md`/`squadB.md`, the "14 integrations" figure, or `sharedAiBrainBrief.md` at face value in future work here — cross-check against CODEOWNERS / `.claude/registry/` / `.mcp.json` as the more current, mechanically-enforced sources. See [[project-manndotfiles]] for the separate personal-vs-project Claude Code config distinction (manndotfiles = Marcel's global tool config; this repo's `.claude/` + `AGENTS.md` = the team's shared project contract).

## Re-audit report

**Verdict: solid now, but this pass found and fixed real problems — it wasn't just a clean confirmation.** I re-read the current playbook myself, personally verified the highest-stakes claims directly against both repos (not just trusting the earlier research), and sent an independent agent to specifically try to break the skill-by-skill claims rather than confirm them. That combination caught things a friendlier pass would have missed.

**What was actually wrong and is now fixed (7 edits):**

1. **A third stale "Section 10" reference**, in §0's "Scale gap" bullet — my first round's cleanup grep was case-sensitive and missed the capitalized "Section 10." Fixed, and re-verified case-insensitively this time.
2. **The Contentful row overclaimed.** `contentful-register-component`/`contentful-drift-check` both assume a co-located `*ContentfulDefinition.ts` file per component — but the 3 components actually live in Contentful Studio today are inlined in one array instead, and zero `*ContentfulDefinition.ts` files exist anywhere in the repo. Drift-check currently checks nothing, silently. The playbook was telling you to trust a tool that's currently blind. Corrected.
3. **CODEOWNERS list was incomplete** — there are 5 real teams, not 4 (`pwa-qa-team` was missing). Added.
4. **The squad-ownership contradiction (§16.4 #1) was underspecified.** Direct reads found `squadA.md`/`squadB.md` both self-label *"Draft squad split — scope can still change"* — real evidence they may be the stale side, not a coin-flip. And the independent skill-audit found `onboarding`'s actual interactive script unconditionally tells a new Squad B hire they own PDP/PLP — meaning this isn't just a documentation disagreement, it's live misinformation a new hire would receive today. Rewrote the point to carry this weight without declaring a final winner — that's still the leads' call.
5. **Added a 4th gap-hunt, verified by literally running the command:** `/code-quality`'s documented default (`git diff --name-only main`) throws `fatal: ambiguous argument 'main'` in this repo — there's no local `main` branch. `/pr-checklist` gets it right (diffs `develop`). Now §16.4 has four contradictions, not three, and the closing paragraph and intro count were updated to match.
6. Fixed a leftover singular/plural mismatch in §16.5 ("contradiction" → "contradictions").

**Re-confirmed accurate, no change needed:** the settings.seed.json effort dial and plugin list, the "no personal instructions file" claim, squadA.md/squadB.md's actual page lists, all 5 hook script names, the `.mcp.json` config, all `.github/workflows/` names, the 18-integration count (my own quick grep undercounted at first — the direct file read confirms 18, table-verified), the `docs/` dead-path claim in the three prompt templates, and 9 of the 13 skill-behavior claims in §16.1.

**Verified true but deliberately not added to the document** (diminishing returns — these don't change any conclusion, and the doc is already dense): `session-start`'s own memory table mislocates `architecture.md` and references a `.docs/memory/userProfile.md` that doesn't exist anywhere; `project-init` still assumes a stale `ZIM` Jira prefix when the repo already uses `SFCC`; `audit-tier`'s blast-radius check is a plain grep, not a real import-graph. All logged in the `[[project-zimmermann-pwa]]` memory in case they matter later.

Nothing left that needs your input right now — the four gap-hunt items in §16.4 are supposed to stay unresolved (that's the point of the section). Let me know if you want me to go the other direction and actually raise any of them with the real leads or fix the underlying repo bugs (the `code-quality` default and the Contentful convention mismatch are both quick, real fixes if you want them).
